    public FakeRaiseEventCall(byte code, object? data, int actorId = 1)
    {
        Request = new RaiseEventRequest { EventCode = code, Data = data };
        ActorId = actorId;
    }

    public int ActorId { get; }

    public RaiseEventRequest Request { get; }

    public FakeOutcome Outcome { get; private set; }

    public string? Message { get; private set; }

    public bool IsProcessed => Outcome != FakeOutcome.Pending;

    public void Continue() => Outcome = FakeOutcome.Continued;

    public void Fail(string message)
    {
        Outcome = FakeOutcome.Failed;
        Message = message;
    }

    public void Cancel() => Outcome = FakeOutcome.Cancelled;
}

public sealed class FakeHost : IPluginHost
{
    public List<(byte Code, object? Data)> Broadcasts { get; } = new();

    public string RoomName { get; set; } = "test-room";

    public IReadOnlyList<IActor> Actors { get; } = Array.Empty<IActor>();

    public int MasterClientId { get; set; } = 1;

    public PropertyTable RoomProperties { get; } = new();

    public ILogger Logger { get; } = NullLogger.Instance;

    public long ServerTimeMs { get; set; }

    public IReadOnlyCollection<INetworkObject> NetworkObjects { get; } = Array.Empty<INetworkObject>();

    public IActor? GetActor(int actorId) => null;

    public INetworkObject? GetNetworkObject(int viewId) => null;

    public void BroadcastEvent(byte code, object? data, ReceiverGroup receivers = ReceiverGroup.All, int[]? targets = null, CachingOption caching = CachingOption.DoNotCache, DeliveryMode delivery = DeliveryMode.ReliableOrdered, int senderActorId = 0) =>
        Broadcasts.Add((code, data));

    public void SetRoomProperties(PropertyTable props, bool broadcast = true) => RoomProperties.Merge(props);

    public void SetPlayerProperties(int actorId, PropertyTable props, bool broadcast = true)
    {
    }

    public void KickActor(int actorId, string reason)
    {
    }

    public void CloseRoom()
    {
    }

    public IDisposable CreateTimer(TimeSpan dueTime, TimeSpan period, Action callback) => new NoopDisposable();

    public IDisposable CreateTimer(TimeSpan dueTime, TimeSpan period, Func<CancellationToken, ValueTask> callback) => new NoopDisposable();

    public void Enqueue(Action action) => action();

    public Task<HttpResponseMessage> HttpAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken ct = default) =>
        Task.FromException<HttpResponseMessage>(new InvalidOperationException("No HTTP in unit tests"));

    public void RunInBackground(Func<CancellationToken, Task> work)
    {
    }

    private sealed class NoopDisposable : IDisposable
    {
        public void Dispose()
        {
        }
    }
}

With the fakes in place, a test is short:

ScoreCapTests.cs
namespace ScoreCap.Tests;

public sealed class ScoreCapTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Event_within_the_cap_continues()
    {
        var plugin = new ScoreCapPlugin(new FakeHost());
        var call = new FakeRaiseEventCall(ScoreCapPlugin.ScoreEvent, 50);

        await plugin.OnRaiseEventAsync(call, CancellationToken.None);

        Assert.Equal(FakeOutcome.Continued, call.Outcome);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Event_above_the_cap_fails_with_a_message()
    {
        var plugin = new ScoreCapPlugin(new FakeHost());
        var call = new FakeRaiseEventCall(ScoreCapPlugin.ScoreEvent, 500);

        await plugin.OnRaiseEventAsync(call, CancellationToken.None);

        Assert.Equal(FakeOutcome.Failed, call.Outcome);
        Assert.Contains("100", call.Message);
    }
}

Fakes cannot reproduce the room fiber, timeouts or real delivery. Keep logic that is worth testing in plain methods and keep hooks thin.

docs.title: Level 3: the real server in a test
docs.text:
ServerHost.Build creates the same host as Program.cs. A test can start it on a random port, register a plugin factory in code instead of a folder, and connect with BotClient from the test client project. The repository's own tests use this approach.

ServerTests.cs
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using NetPulse.Common;
using NetPulse.Server.Hosting;
using NetPulse.Server.Networking;
using NetPulse.Server.Plugins;
using NetPulse.TestClient;

namespace ScoreCap.Tests;

public sealed class ServerTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IHost? _host;
    private BotClient? _bot;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        var settings = new Dictionary<string, string?>
        {
            ["NetPulse:Port"] = "0",
            ["NetPulse:EnableConsole"] = "false",
            ["NetPulse:Plugins:HotReload"] = "false",
            ["NetPulse:Plugins:Directory"] = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "netpulse-test-plugins"),
            ["Logging:LogLevel:Default"] = "Warning"
        };

        _host = ServerHost.Build(Array.Empty<string>(), settings);
        _host.Services.GetRequiredService<PluginManager>().Register("ScoreCap", new ScoreCapFactory());
        await _host.StartAsync();

        _bot = new BotClient("bot");
        await _bot.ConnectAsync("127.0.0.1", _host.Services.GetRequiredService<NetPulseServer>().Port);
        await _bot.AuthenticateAsync();
        await _bot.JoinOrCreateRoomAsync("room", new RoomOptions { Plugin = "ScoreCap" });
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _bot?.Dispose();

        if (_host is not null)
        {
            await _host.StopAsync();
            _host.Dispose();
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Server_rejects_an_oversized_score_event()
    {
        var response = await _bot!.RaiseEventAsync(ScoreCapPlugin.ScoreEvent, 500);

        Assert.Equal(ReturnCode.PluginReportedError, response.ReturnCode);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Server_accepts_a_small_score_event()
    {
        var response = await _bot!.RaiseEventAsync(ScoreCapPlugin.ScoreEvent, 5);

        Assert.Equal(ReturnCode.Ok, response.ReturnCode);
    }
}

RaiseEventAsync sets a request id, so the server always answers it. Real clients that raise events without a request id get no answer unless the event fails.

The project file for the tests references the SDK projects, the server and the test client:

ScoreCap.Tests.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <IsPackable>false</IsPackable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk" Version="17.14.1" />
    <PackageReference Include="xunit" Version="2.9.3" />
    <PackageReference Include="xunit.runner.visualstudio" Version="3.1.4" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Using Include="Xunit" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Server\NetPulse.Server.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="path\to\NetPulse_Server\tools\NetPulse.TestClient\NetPulse.TestClient.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Put ScoreCapPlugin.cs in the same project, or reference your plugin project from it. Run the tests with dotnet test.

docs.title: Timers, HTTP and background work
docs.text: Hooks run when a player does something. Plugins also need work that happens on its own schedule or outside the room's queue. The host offers four tools for it: timers, Enqueue, HttpAsync and RunInBackground.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
IDisposable CreateTimer(TimeSpan dueTime, TimeSpan period, Action callback);
IDisposable CreateTimer(TimeSpan dueTime, TimeSpan period, Func<CancellationToken, ValueTask> callback);
  • The callback first runs after dueTime. A zero or negative dueTime runs it right away.
  • If period is positive, the callback repeats at that interval. A zero, negative or Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan period makes the timer fire once.
  • Callbacks run on the room fiber, so they can touch room state without locks.
  • A tick never starts while the previous callback is still running. If a callback takes longer than the period, the missed ticks do not pile up.
  • The Func overload lets the callback await. While it waits, the room keeps handling messages: a timer callback is not a queue item, so it never holds up the room, but other code can run between its awaits.
  • An exception in a callback goes to OnUnhandledExceptionAsync. The timer keeps running.
  • Call Dispose() on the returned object to stop the timer. The room also stops all its timers when it closes.

A countdown that starts when the first player joins:

CountdownPlugin.cs
using NetPulse.Plugins;

namespace TimerExamples;

public sealed class CountdownPlugin : RoomPlugin
{
    public const byte CountdownEvent = 80;
    private const int Seconds = 10;

    private IDisposable? _timer;
    private int _remaining = Seconds;

    public CountdownPlugin(IPluginHost host)
        : base(host)
    {
    }

    public override ValueTask OnJoinAsync(IJoinCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        _timer ??= Host.CreateTimer(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TickAsync);
        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }

    public override ValueTask OnCloseRoomAsync(ICloseRoomCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        _timer?.Dispose();
        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }

    private ValueTask TickAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        _remaining--;
        Host.BroadcastEvent(CountdownEvent, _remaining);

        if (_remaining <= 0)
        {
            _timer?.Dispose();
            _timer = null;
        }

        return default;
    }
}

docs.title: Enqueue
docs.text:
void Enqueue(Action action);

Enqueue puts an action at the end of the room's queue. It runs after the item that is running now has finished, on the room fiber. Use it to:

  • come back to the fiber from a thread you started;
  • do something after the current hook's action completes, such as sending a message after a join response (see Writing a plugin);
  • split a long job into steps so that other messages can run in between.

It is safe to call from any thread. An exception in the action goes to OnUnhandledExceptionAsync. If the room has already closed, the call does nothing.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
Task<HttpResponseMessage> HttpAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken ct = default);

HttpAsync sends a request through the server's IHttpClientFactory, so connections are pooled and shared. The client has a fixed timeout of 15 seconds. The HookTimeoutMs limit applies to a hook that awaits it, so pass the hook's ct to cut the request off when the hook times out.

Awaited inside a hook, the call keeps the room waiting and you resume on the fiber. Hooks has two examples, a ban check and a result upload. The method can throw HttpRequestException or TaskCanceledException; decide whether a failed call should reject the action or let it through.

It is also safe to call outside the fiber, for example from RunInBackground.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text:
void RunInBackground(Func<CancellationToken, Task> work);

RunInBackground starts the work on the thread pool, off the room fiber. The room does not wait for it. Use it when the result does not change the outcome of a call: analytics, webhooks, saving a statistic.

  • The token is cancelled when the room closes. An OperationCanceledException after that is ignored.
  • Any other exception is logged as Background work in room X failed. It does not reach OnUnhandledExceptionAsync.
  • Background code runs outside the fiber. Do not read Actors, RoomProperties or other room state from it. Read what you need first, on the fiber, and capture it in the closure.
  • To report a result back, call Host.Enqueue, or one of BroadcastEvent, SetRoomProperties, SetPlayerProperties, KickActor or CloseRoom. They hand the work to the fiber for you.

A plugin that posts each chat message to a webhook without delaying the chat, and announces a failure to the room:

WebhookPlugin.cs
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using NetPulse.Plugins;

namespace TimerExamples;

public sealed class WebhookPlugin : RoomPlugin
{
    private const byte ChatEvent = 20;
    private const byte NoticeEvent = 71;

    private readonly string _webhookUrl;

    public WebhookPlugin(IPluginHost host, string webhookUrl)
        : base(host) => _webhookUrl = webhookUrl;

    public override ValueTask OnRaiseEventAsync(IRaiseEventCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (info.Request.EventCode == ChatEvent && info.Request.Data is string text)
        {
            var room = Host.RoomName;
            var author = Host.GetActor(info.ActorId)?.NickName ?? "unknown";
            Host.RunInBackground(token => PostAsync(room, author, text, token));
        }

        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }

    private async Task PostAsync(string room, string author, string text, CancellationToken token)
    {
        using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, _webhookUrl)
        {
            Content = JsonContent.Create(new { room, author, text })
        };

        using var response = await Host.HttpAsync(request, token);

        if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
        {
            Host.BroadcastEvent(NoticeEvent, "The chat log is unavailable");
        }
    }
}

If PostAsync throws, the server logs it and the room carries on.

docs.title: Choosing a tool
docs.text: You want to Use Do something every N seconds, or once later CreateTimer Wait for an HTTP answer before deciding a hook await Host.HttpAsync(request, ct) in the hook Fire and forget slow work RunInBackground Return to the room from other code, or run after the current item Enqueue

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text: This walkthrough builds a small plugin from an empty project to one that the server has loaded. The plugin greets each player who joins and masks banned words in chat messages.

docs.title: 1. Create the project
docs.text:
You need the .NET 10 SDK and a checkout of the server repository, because the plugin references the NetPulse.Plugins and NetPulse.Common projects from it.

dotnet new classlib -n GreeterPlugin -f net10.0
cd GreeterPlugin
rm Class1.cs

Replace the contents of GreeterPlugin.csproj. Change path\to\NetPulse_Server to the location of your checkout:

GreeterPlugin.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Plugins\NetPulse.Plugins.csproj" Private="false" />
    <ProjectReference Include="path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Common\NetPulse.Common.csproj" Private="false" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" Version="10.0.14" PrivateAssets="all" ExcludeAssets="runtime" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <None Include="plugin.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Private="false" keeps the SDK assemblies out of your output. The host always supplies its own copies of NetPulse.Plugins, NetPulse.Common, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions and Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions, and ignores any copy in the plugin folder. The logging package is referenced only so the plugin compiles.

If you cannot reference the projects, build the repository once and reference the dlls instead:

<ItemGroup>
  <Reference Include="NetPulse.Plugins">
    <HintPath>path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Plugins\bin\Release\net10.0\NetPulse.Plugins.dll</HintPath>
    <Private>false</Private>
  </Reference>
  <Reference Include="NetPulse.Common">
    <HintPath>path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Common\bin\Release\netstandard2.1\NetPulse.Common.dll</HintPath>
    <Private>false</Private>
  </Reference>
</ItemGroup>

docs.title: 2. Write the factory and the plugin
docs.text:
A plugin has two classes. The factory reads the configuration and creates one plugin object per room. The plugin derives from RoomPlugin and overrides the hooks it needs.

GreeterPlugin.cs
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using NetPulse.Common;
using NetPulse.Plugins;

namespace GreeterPlugin;

public sealed class GreeterFactory : IPluginFactory
{
    public ValueTask<PluginCreateResult> CreateAsync(IPluginHost host, string pluginName, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> config, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var greeting = config.TryGetValue("Greeting", out var value) ? value : "Welcome";
        var banned = config.TryGetValue("BannedWords", out var raw)
            ? raw.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries | StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries)
            : Array.Empty<string>();

        return ValueTask.FromResult(PluginCreateResult.Ok(new GreeterPlugin(host, greeting, banned)));
    }
}

public sealed class GreeterPlugin : RoomPlugin
{
    public const byte ChatEvent = 20;
    public const byte GreetingEvent = 60;

    private readonly string _greeting;
    private readonly string[] _banned;

    public GreeterPlugin(IPluginHost host, string greeting, string[] banned)
        : base(host)
    {
        _greeting = greeting;
        _banned = banned;
    }

    public override ValueTask OnJoinAsync(IJoinCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var actorId = info.Actor.ActorId;
        var text = $"{_greeting}, {info.Actor.NickName}!";

        Host.Enqueue(() => Host.BroadcastEvent(
            GreetingEvent,
            text,
            ReceiverGroup.Targets,
            new[]
            {
                actorId
            }));

        Host.Logger.LogInformation("Greeted {Nick} in room {Room}", info.Actor.NickName, Host.RoomName);
        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }

    public override ValueTask OnRaiseEventAsync(IRaiseEventCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (info.Request.EventCode == ChatEvent && info.Request.Data is string message)
        {
            info.Request.Data = Mask(message);
        }

        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }

    private string Mask(string message)
    {
        foreach (var word in _banned)
        {
            message = message.Replace(word, new string('*', word.Length), StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        }

        return message;
    }
}

What happens here:

  • CreateAsync returns a PluginCreateResult. Use PluginCreateResult.Failed("reason") to refuse to create the room's plugin; the client then gets PluginReportedError.
  • OnJoinAsync runs after the player has been added to the room but before the server sends the join response. A message sent from inside the hook would reach the client before it knows it is in the room, so the plugin uses Host.Enqueue to send the greeting after the join has finished.
  • Every hook must call Continue(), Fail(message) or, where offered, Cancel() before it returns. A hook that returns without deciding is logged as an error and counts as Fail.
  • info.Request is mutable. Changing Data in OnRaiseEventAsync changes what the other players receive.
  • The hooks are ValueTask methods. When there is nothing to await, return default.

docs.title: 3. Add the manifest
docs.text:
Create plugin.json next to the project file. The csproj copies it to the output.

plugin.json
{
  "name": "GreeterPlugin",
  "assembly": "GreeterPlugin.dll",
  "factory": "GreeterPlugin.GreeterFactory"
}

name is what rooms and the configuration use. factory is the full name of the factory class, namespace included.

docs.title: 4. Build and install
docs.text:
dotnet publish -c Release -o out

Copy the result into a folder named after the plugin, inside the server's plugin directory:

Running from sourcePublished server 
mkdir -p path/to/NetPulse_Server/src/NetPulse.Server/bin/Debug/net10.0/plugins/GreeterPlugin
cp out/GreeterPlugin.dll out/GreeterPlugin.pdb out/plugin.json path/to/NetPulse_Server/src/NetPulse.Server/bin/Debug/net10.0/plugins/GreeterPlugin/

mkdir -p publish/plugins/GreeterPlugin
cp out/GreeterPlugin.dll out/GreeterPlugin.pdb out/plugin.json publish/plugins/GreeterPlugin/

If the server is already running with hot reload on, it picks up the new folder by itself within a second.

docs.title: 5. Turn it on
docs.text:
Rooms use the plugin when RoomOptions.Plugin names it, or when it is the default plugin. To make it the default and pass settings, add this to appsettings.json:

{
  "NetPulse": {
    "Plugins": {
      "Default": "GreeterPlugin",
      "Settings": {
        "GreeterPlugin": {
          "Greeting": "Hello",
          "BannedWords": "darn,heck"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Environment variables work as well: NetPulse__Plugins__Default=GreeterPlugin.

From Unity, a single room can ask for it:

var room = await Pulse.JoinOrCreateRoom("lobby-1", new RoomOptions { MaxPlayers = 8, Plugin = "GreeterPlugin" });

docs.title: 6. Check that it loaded
docs.text:
Start the server and look for the load message:

info: NetPulse.Server.Plugins.PluginManager[0] Loaded plugin GreeterPlugin v2 from GreeterPlugin

Run plugins in the server console to list it. Then join a room. The server log shows Greeted Alice in room lobby-1, and the joining client receives event 60 with the greeting text. Chat messages sent as event 20 reach the other players with the banned words masked.

If the plugin does not load, see the troubleshooting list in Operations. To test hooks without a game client, see Testing.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Hooks describes every hook and the rules for Continue, Fail and Cancel.
  • Host API lists everything the plugin can do to its room.
  • Timers, HTTP and background work covers work that happens outside a hook.

docs.title: Codes and keys
docs.text: Every table on this page comes from NetPulse.Common (Codes.cs, Enums.cs and RoomPropertyKeys.cs). How they are used on the wire is described in Wire protocol.

docs.title: Operation codes
docs.text: Code Name Purpose 1 Authenticate Log in. Must be the first operation. 2 JoinLobby Subscribe to the room list. 3 LeaveLobby Unsubscribe from the room list. 10 CreateRoom Create a room and join it. 11 JoinRoom Join an existing room by name. 12 JoinOrCreateRoom Join a room, creating it if it does not exist. 13 JoinRandomRoom Join a random open room that matches a filter. 14 LeaveRoom Leave the current room. 20 RaiseEvent Send an event to other players. 21 SetRoomProperties Change room properties. 22 SetPlayerProperties Change player properties. 23 ChangeInterestGroups Join or leave interest groups. 24 TransferOwnership Give a network object to another player. 25 RequestOwnership Ask for ownership of a network object. 26 RegisterSceneObjects Master only: declare the ownership modes of scene objects. 30 GetRoomList Get the current room list.

docs.title: Event codes
docs.text:
Code Name Sent by Meaning 0 to 199 your own events clients, plugins EventCode.MaxUserEvent is 199. 230 RoomList server Full room list or a delta. 231 PlayerJoined server Another player joined. 232 PlayerLeft server A player left or became inactive. 233 RoomPropertiesChanged server Room property delta. 234 PlayerPropertiesChanged server Player property delta. 235 MasterClientChanged server A new master client. 236 OwnershipChanged server A network object changed owner. 237 OwnershipRequested server Sent to the owner of a Request-mode object. 240 ObjectInstantiate clients A network object was created. 241 ObjectDestroy clients A network object was destroyed. 242 Rpc clients A remote procedure call. 243 StateSync clients State of an object, from its owner. 244 Message clients A typed message. 245 SyncVarSet clients A master-owned sync variable changed (master only). 250 ErrorInfo server A warning or error notice with ErrorCode and Message.

Clients may raise codes 0 to 199 and 240 to 245. Every other code is reserved and fails with Forbidden. A plugin can broadcast any code.

docs.title: Return codes
docs.text: Code Name Meaning 0 Ok Success. -1 InternalError An unexpected server error. -2 InvalidRequest Malformed request, unknown operation, a second join in progress, or the user is already in that room. -3 NotAuthenticated Authenticate first. -4 NotInRoom The operation needs a room. -5 AlreadyInRoom The peer is already in a room. -6 Forbidden Not allowed: a reserved event or property, or a failed ownership check. -10 RoomNotFound No such room, or the room closed while joining. -11 RoomFull The room has reached MaxPlayers. -12 RoomClosed The room is not open. Also the ErrorInfo code sent when a room closes. -13 RoomAlreadyExists CreateRoom with a name that is taken. -14 NoMatchFound JoinRandomRoom found nothing and had no options to create a room. -15 PropertyCasFailed The expected properties did not match. -16 ActorNotFound The target player is not in the room. -17 ObjectNotFound The view id is not registered. -20 PluginReportedError A plugin refused the action. The message is the plugin's. -21 PluginNotFound The room asked for a plugin that is not installed. -30 VersionMismatch Different protocol version. -31 InvalidAppId The AppId does not match the server's. -32 AuthenticationFailed The authentication plugin refused the client.

RaiseEvent for an instantiate: byte 49 TickRate Join response: int 50 IsFullList RoomList: bool 51 Rooms RoomList: object[] 52 RemovedRooms RoomList: string[] 53 IsInactive Player info: bool 54 docs.title: Value type codes
docs.text:
Code Name 0 Null 1 Bool 2 Byte 3 Short 4 Int 5 Long 6 Float 7 Double 8 String 9 ByteArray 10 IntArray 11 FloatArray 12 StringArray 13 ObjectArray 14 Dictionary 15 PropertyTable 16 Guid 17 ParameterDictionary 18 Extended 100 to 199 Custom types (CustomMin, CustomMax)

The Unity package uses 100 to 105 for Vector2, Vector3, Quaternion, Color, Vector2Int and Vector3Int. Payload layouts are in Wire protocol.

docs.title: Enumerations
docs.text: Enum Values MessageKind 1 OperationRequest, 2 OperationResponse, 3 Event, 4 Ping, 5 Pong DeliveryMode 0 ReliableOrdered, 1 ReliableUnordered, 2 UnreliableSequenced, 3 Unreliable ReceiverGroup 0 Others, 1 All, 2 MasterClient, 3 Targets CachingOption 0 DoNotCache, 1 AddToRoomCache, 2 AddToRoomCacheGlobal, 3 RemoveFromRoomCache, 4 RemoveFromCacheForActorsLeft ObjectOwnershipMode 0 Fixed, 1 Takeover, 2 Request ObjectFlag 1 PersistAcrossScenes (a bit flag in ObjectFlags)

docs.title: Reserved room property keys
docs.text:
Only the master client may set these keys. See Security.

Key Constant Type Meaning _isOpen RoomPropertyKeys.IsOpen bool Whether new players can join. _isVisible RoomPropertyKeys.IsVisible bool Whether the room is in the lobby list. _maxPlayers RoomPropertyKeys.MaxPlayers int, 0 to 255 The player limit. _scene RoomPropertyKeys.Scene string The current network scene. A change removes scene-bound objects.

docs.title: View ids
docs.text: Range Meaning 1 to 999 Scene objects. Owned by the master client unless assigned. 1000 and up Objects created by players. viewId / 1000 is the creator's actor id, so actor 3 owns 3000 to 3999.

docs.title: Wire protocol
docs.text: This page describes what travels between a client and the server, for anyone writing a custom client. Unity users never need it. All numbers are from protocol version 1 (Protocol.ProtocolVersion). The names come from NetPulse.Common, a library that compiles on .NET Standard 2.1 and ships inside the Unity package. A .NET client can use it directly.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
NetPulse sends its messages over UDP with LiteNetLib 1.3.5. A custom client has to speak LiteNetLib's protocol, so in practice it is a .NET client that uses the same LiteNetLib version.

  • The client connects to the server's UDP port (5055 by default) with a connection key (NetPulse by default). The key is checked by the transport.
  • Each NetPulse message is one LiteNetLib packet, sent on the default channel.
  • The delivery mode of a packet maps to a LiteNetLib method:
DeliveryMode Value LiteNetLib method ReliableOrdered 0 ReliableOrdered ReliableUnordered 1 ReliableUnordered UnreliableSequenced 2 Sequenced Unreliable 3 Unreliable

The server sends responses and most events with ReliableOrdered. Events raised by clients or plugins are sent with the Delivery the sender asked for. Pongs are Unreliable.

  • The server drops a peer that is silent for DisconnectTimeoutMs (10 seconds by default). Keep calling PollEvents, which sends the transport's keep-alive messages.
  • When the server disconnects a client on purpose, it puts a UTF-8 reason in the disconnect data. Known reasons are Overloaded and AuthenticationFailed.

docs.title: Encrypted transport
docs.text:
When the server runs with Encryption:Mode set to Optional or Required, an encrypting client wraps every UDP datagram of the LiteNetLib stream in a record. Nothing above the transport changes: the messages described below are the plaintext inside the records. With Disabled, or for a plain client on an Optional server, the datagrams are exactly the LiteNetLib datagrams described above. The reference implementation is NetPulse.Common/Security, which has no dependency on LiteNetLib.

Discriminator. The low five bits of the first byte of a LiteNetLib packet are its packet property, which is always below 0x1F. A NetPulse record has 0x1F in those five bits, so the two kinds are told apart by the first byte:

First byte Record Direction 0x1F Init client to server 0x3F Retry server to client 0x5F Response server to client 0x7F Data both 0xFF Data with padding both

Algorithms. There is no negotiation. The handshake is the Noise pattern NK with the server's static key pinned: Noise_NK_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256, or Noise_NKpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 when a pre-shared key is used, with the prologue 0x1F 0x01 followed by the 4-byte key id. The key id is the first 4 bytes of the SHA-256 of the server's public key. The result is two ChaCha20-Poly1305 keys, one per direction, and the handshake hash.

Handshake.

Init     = 0x1F | version (1) | key id (4) | cookie length (1: 0 or 16) | cookie | Noise message 1 (48) | zero padding
Retry    = 0x3F | cookie length (16) | cookie (16)
Response = 0x5F | Noise message 2 (48)

An Init is padded to at least 96 bytes. Both replies are shorter than the request. The cookie is the first 16 bytes of HMAC-SHA256(secret, address (16) | port (2, big-endian) | epoch (8)); the address is the IPv6 form, with an IPv4 address written as ::ffff:a.b.c.d. A client that has no cookie sends an empty one, receives a Retry, and sends the Init again with the cookie, and the server does the key agreement only then. The client replaces its first LiteNetLib connect request with the Init, so the transport's own retransmissions repeat the handshake. After the Response, the client sends its connect request in a Data record.

Data record.

type (1) | epoch (1) | counter (8, little-endian) | ciphertext | tag (16)

The 10 header bytes are the associated data, the nonce is four zero bytes followed by the counter, and each direction has its own key. The overhead is 26 bytes. In a padded record (type 0xFF) the plaintext is the payload, zero bytes, and a 2-byte little-endian count of those zero bytes, and the whole record is a multiple of the padding block. The counter starts at 0 for each direction and only grows. The receiver keeps a sliding window (4096 packets by default), checks the tag first and moves the window only after the tag is valid.

Rekeying. Each direction replaces its key by HKDF-Expand(key, "rekey", 32) and increments the epoch byte. The receiver accepts the next four epochs ahead, which covers packet loss, and keeps the previous key until the replay window has passed it.

Errors. The server answers a malformed or unverifiable record with nothing. A client that gets no reply sees only a timeout.

docs.title: Primitives
docs.text:
All multi-byte numbers are little-endian.

Name Encoding byte, bool 1 byte. A bool is 0 or 1. short, ushort 2 bytes. int, uint, float 4 bytes. long, ulong, double 8 bytes. varuint 7 bits per byte, low bits first, the high bit marks "more bytes follow". At most 5 bytes. string varuint (UTF-8 byte count + 1), then the bytes. A prefix of 0 is null, a prefix of 1 is the empty string. bytes varuint length, then the bytes. Guid 16 bytes in the .NET layout.

docs.title: Message framing
docs.text:
The first byte of every packet is the message kind.

Kind Value Layout after the kind byte OperationRequest 1 opCode: byte, requestId: ushort, parameters OperationResponse 2 opCode: byte, requestId: ushort, returnCode: short, debugMessage: string, parameters Event 3 code: byte, parameters Ping 4 clientTicks: long, serverTicks: long Pong 5 clientTicks: long, serverMs: long

A response carries the opCode and requestId of its request. returnCode 0 is success; the others are in Codes and keys. debugMessage is human-readable text.

For a ping, send your own clock in clientTicks and 0 in serverTicks. The server answers with your value and its own time in milliseconds since it started. Subtract to estimate the round trip and the clock offset.

Request ids are yours to choose. Use a non-zero id for every request you want answered. The server answers every operation except RaiseEvent: that one gets an answer only when the id is non-zero or the event fails.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameters is a dictionary from a one-byte key to a value:

varuint count
count x ( key: byte, value )

The keys are the ParamKey constants, listed in Codes and keys. Missing keys read as defaults. The server converts between numeric types when it reads a parameter, so sending an int where a byte is expected works as long as the value fits.

docs.title: Value types
docs.text:
Every value starts with a type code byte, followed by its payload.

Code Type Payload 0 null none 1 bool 1 byte 2 byte 1 byte 3 short 2 bytes 4 int 4 bytes 5 long 8 bytes 6 float 4 bytes 7 double 8 bytes 8 string string 9 byte[] bytes 10 int[] varuint count, then 4 bytes per element 11 float[] varuint count, then 4 bytes per element 12 string[] varuint count, then that many string values 13 object[] varuint count, then that many values 14 dictionary varuint count, then (string key, value) pairs 15 PropertyTable same layout as a dictionary 16 Guid 16 bytes 17 ParameterDictionary a parameters block (count, then key and value pairs) 18 extended ushort id, varuint length, then the payload 100 to 199 custom varuint length, then the payload

Values nest up to 16 levels deep. A declared count or length larger than the data left in the packet makes the packet invalid.

Codes 100 to 199 and 18 carry application types such as vectors. They are length-prefixed so the server can store and forward a type it does not know: it keeps the bytes as an OpaqueValue and writes them back unchanged. The Unity package registers Vector2 (100), Vector3 (101), Quaternion (102), Color (103), Vector2Int (104) and Vector3Int (105). In .NET, register your own with NetTypeRegistry.Register (codes 100 to 199) or NetTypeRegistry.RegisterExtended (ids 0 to 65535).

A malformed packet is logged and ignored.

docs.title: A session
docs.text:
1. Connect with the connection key.
  2. Send Authenticate (op 1) with the AppId, protocol version, user id, nickname and optional token. Until it succeeds, every other operation returns NotAuthenticated.
  3. Optionally send JoinLobby (op 2). The server answers and then sends the full room list as event 230. Later events 230 carry changes (IsFullList false) at the RoomListIntervalMs interval. GetRoomList (op 30) returns the full list in the response.
  4. Create or join a room with op 10, 11, 12 or 13. Only one join may be in progress per peer.
  5. Inside the room, use ops 14 to 26. Events arrive as they happen.

docs.title: Operations and their parameters
docs.text:
Op Name Parameters 1 Authenticate AppId (str), ProtocolVersion (int), AppVersion (str), UserId (str), NickName (str), AuthToken (str), AuthData (PropertyTable) 2 JoinLobby LobbyName (str) 3 LeaveLobby none 10 CreateRoom RoomName, Options (ParameterDictionary), PlayerProperties (PropertyTable) 11 JoinRoom RoomName, PlayerProperties 12 JoinOrCreateRoom like CreateRoom 13 JoinRandomRoom ExpectedProperties, ExpectedMaxPlayers (byte), PlayerProperties, Options (used if a room has to be created) 14 LeaveRoom BecomeInactive (bool) 20 RaiseEvent EventCode (byte), Data, Receivers (byte), TargetActors (int[]), InterestGroup (byte), Caching (byte), Delivery (byte), ViewId (int), OwnershipMode (byte), ObjectFlags (byte) 21 SetRoomProperties Properties, ExpectedProperties, Broadcast (bool, default true) 22 SetPlayerProperties ActorId (0 means yourself), Properties, ExpectedProperties, Broadcast 23 ChangeInterestGroups GroupsToAdd (byte[]), GroupsToRemove (byte[]) 24 TransferOwnership ViewId, NewOwnerActorId 25 RequestOwnership ViewId 26 RegisterSceneObjects ViewIds (int[]), OwnershipModes (byte[]) 30 GetRoomList none

Options for room creation is a parameters block with MaxPlayers (byte, 0 is unlimited), IsVisible, IsOpen, Properties (initial custom room properties), LobbyProperties (string[] of property keys shown in the room list), Plugin, PlayerTtlMs and EmptyRoomTtlMs.

PlayerTtlMs and EmptyRoomTtlMs are in milliseconds. With PlayerTtlMs other than 0, a player who disconnects, or leaves with BecomeInactive, stays in the room as an inactive actor and can rejoin with the same UserId. A positive value removes the inactive player after that time, a negative value keeps it until it rejoins. A positive EmptyRoomTtlMs keeps an empty room alive for that time.

docs.title: Responses
docs.text:
A successful Authenticate returns UserId, NickName, ServerTimeTicks (milliseconds since server start, despite the name) and ProtocolVersion.

The join operations (10 to 13) answer with the room state, or with an error code and no parameters:

Key Content RoomName The room name. ActorId Your actor id. MasterClientId Actor id of the master. Players object[] of parameter blocks, one per actor: ActorId, NickName, UserId, Properties, IsInactive. RoomProperties The room properties, including the reserved keys. ServerTimeTicks Server milliseconds. MaxPlayers, IsOpen, IsVisible Room settings. IsRejoin True when you took over an inactive actor. TickRate The server's TickRate setting.

After the join response the server sends the cached events, then an OwnershipChanged event for each object whose owner differs from its creator. The other players receive PlayerJoined with your player block.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
An event carries a code and a parameters block. Codes up to 199 are your own events, and the object events 240 to 245 are also raised by clients. Both arrive with this payload:

Key Content Sender Actor id of the sender (0 for the server). Data The value the sender passed. ViewId The view id, when there is one.

The server's own events use different payloads:

Code Name Payload keys 230 RoomList IsFullList, Rooms (object[] of blocks with RoomName, PlayerCount, MaxPlayers, IsOpen, Properties), RemovedRooms (string[]) 231 PlayerJoined a player block 232 PlayerLeft ActorId, IsInactive, MasterClientId 233 RoomPropertiesChanged ActorId (0), Properties (the delta, a null value means deleted), Sender 234 PlayerPropertiesChanged ActorId, Properties, Sender 235 MasterClientChanged MasterClientId 236 OwnershipChanged ViewId, NewOwnerActorId (0 for a scene object means "the master"), Sender 237 OwnershipRequested ViewId, RequesterActorId, sent to the owner 250 ErrorInfo ErrorCode, Message

Room and player property changes go to every player, including the one who made them.

docs.title: Receivers, caching and groups
docs.text:
Receivers is 0 Others, 1 All, 2 MasterClient or 3 Targets (the actor ids in TargetActors). A non-zero InterestGroup limits delivery to players who joined that group with ChangeInterestGroups; group 0 reaches everyone.

Caching is 0 DoNotCache, 1 AddToRoomCache, 2 AddToRoomCacheGlobal, 3 RemoveFromRoomCache or 4 RemoveFromCacheForActorsLeft. Cached events are replayed to players who join later. AddToRoomCache events are removed when their sender leaves for good, AddToRoomCacheGlobal events stay. Removing from the cache removes entries with the same event code, and with the same ViewId when you pass one.

docs.title: Network objects
docs.text:
Object events are ordinary RaiseEvent calls with a special code and a ViewId. The server validates them as described in Security: instantiate (240) needs ViewId / 1000 to equal your actor id and a mode in OwnershipMode (0 Fixed, 1 Takeover, 2 Request); ObjectFlags bit 0 marks an object that survives a scene change. Destroy (241) removes the object and its cached events. RPC (242), state sync (243), message (244) and master sync variable (245) are forwarded after their checks. The format of Data for these events belongs to the client and is opaque to the server.

When the room property _scene changes, the server removes every scene object and every object not marked as persistent, with their cached events.

docs.title: A minimal client
docs.text:
This .NET program connects, authenticates and joins a room using NetPulse.Common and LiteNetLib 1.3.5:

WireClient.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="LiteNetLib" Version="1.3.5" />
    <ProjectReference Include="path\to\NetPulse_Server\src\NetPulse.Common\NetPulse.Common.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
MinimalClient.cs
using LiteNetLib;
using NetPulse.Common;

namespace WireExamples;

public sealed class MinimalClient
{
    private readonly NetWriter _writer = new();
    private readonly EventBasedNetListener _listener = new();
    private readonly NetManager _manager;
    private NetPeer? _server;
    private ushort _nextRequestId;

    public MinimalClient()
    {
        _manager = new NetManager(_listener);
        _listener.PeerConnectedEvent += OnConnected;
        _listener.NetworkReceiveEvent += OnReceive;
    }

    public void Run(string host, int port, TimeSpan duration)
    {
        _manager.Start();
        _manager.Connect(host, port, Protocol.DefaultConnectionKey);
        var end = DateTime.UtcNow + duration;

        while (DateTime.UtcNow < end)
        {
            _manager.PollEvents();
            Thread.Sleep(15);
        }

        _manager.Stop();
    }

    private void OnConnected(NetPeer peer)
    {
        _server = peer;
        var login = new AuthenticateRequest { UserId = "demo", NickName = "Demo" };
        Send(OpCode.Authenticate, login.ToParameters());
    }

    private void Send(byte opCode, ParameterDictionary parameters)
    {
        var request = new OperationRequest { OpCode = opCode, RequestId = ++_nextRequestId, Parameters = parameters };
        var packet = Protocol.Serialize(_writer, request);
        _server!.Send(packet.Array!, packet.Offset, packet.Count, DeliveryMethod.ReliableOrdered);
    }

    private void OnReceive(NetPeer peer, NetPacketReader reader, byte channel, DeliveryMethod method)
    {
        var data = new NetReader(reader.GetRemainingBytesSegment());
        var kind = Protocol.ReadKind(data);

        if (kind == MessageKind.OperationResponse)
        {
            var response = Protocol.ReadOperationResponse(data);
            Console.WriteLine($"response op={response.OpCode} request={response.RequestId} code={response.ReturnCode}");

            if (response.OpCode == OpCode.Authenticate && response.ReturnCode == ReturnCode.Ok)
            {
                Send(OpCode.JoinOrCreateRoom, new JoinOrCreateRoomRequest { RoomName = "wire-demo" }.ToParameters());
            }
        }
        else if (kind == MessageKind.Event)
        {
            var received = Protocol.ReadEvent(data);
            Console.WriteLine($"event code={received.Code}");
        }

        reader.Recycle();
    }
}

Start it from a top-level Program.cs:

Program.cs
using WireExamples;

new MinimalClient().Run("127.0.0.1", 5055, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));

Against a running server it prints:

response op=1 request=1 code=0
response op=12 request=2 code=0

Protocol.Serialize returns a segment of the writer's internal buffer, so send it before you reuse the writer.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All options live under the NetPulse section. The server reads appsettings.json from its working directory, then environment variables, then the command line. See Running the server for the syntax of each source.

Out of the box the shipped appsettings.json sets only a few values; every other option takes the default in the tables below.

docs.title: Network and capacity
docs.text: Key Default Effect NetPulse:Port 5055 UDP port the server binds. 0 picks a random free port, which the startup log prints. NetPulse:ConnectionKey NetPulse LiteNetLib connection key. A client with a different key is rejected before it can send anything. The Unity client uses the same default and has a matching field in its settings. NetPulse:MaxConnections 2000 Maximum number of connected peers. New connection requests above the limit are rejected. NetPulse:TickRate 30 Update rate of the transport, in ticks per second (the interval is 1000 / TickRate ms, at least 1 ms). The value is also sent to every client in the join response, and the Unity client uses it for its network tick. Values below 1 are treated as 1. NetPulse:DisconnectTimeoutMs 10000 A peer that sends nothing for this long is dropped. NetPulse:RoomListIntervalMs 1000 How often the lobby sends room list changes to subscribed clients. Values below 50 are treated as 50.

docs.title: Application checks
docs.text:
Key Default Effect NetPulse:AppId empty When set, every client must send exactly this AppId in its authenticate request, otherwise it gets InvalidAppId (-31). When empty, any AppId is accepted. NetPulse:AppVersionCheck true When true, the protocol version sent by the client must equal the server's (currently 1), otherwise the client gets VersionMismatch (-30). The check compares the protocol version, not the AppVersion string of your game.

The AppId is not a secret, because it ships inside your game. Use it to keep unrelated games and test builds apart, and use authentication to decide who may play. See Security.

docs.title: Flood protection and timeouts
docs.text: Key Default Effect NetPulse:PeerQueueLimit 256 Maximum messages one peer may have queued and not yet processed, counted across the lobby and its room. When a peer goes above it, the message is dropped and the peer is disconnected with the reason Overloaded. Values below 1 are treated as 1. NetPulse:RoomQueueCapacity 4096 Hard bound on peer messages queued in one room, and separately in the lobby. When it is full, the new message is dropped and the peer with the most queued messages in that queue is disconnected. That peer is not always the one that just sent. Work the server queues itself (timers, Host.Enqueue, shutdown) is exempt. Values below 1 are treated as 1. NetPulse:OwnershipRequestTimeoutMs 5000 How long an ownership request for a Request-mode object waits for the owner to approve before it expires. Values below 1 are treated as 1. NetPulse:ShutdownTimeoutMs 10000 Time budget for closing all rooms when the server stops.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Transport encryption lives under NetPulse:Encryption. The default Disabled installs nothing and leaves the wire format as it was. See Security for what the modes mean and Deployment for rotating keys.

Key Default Effect NetPulse:Encryption:Mode Disabled Disabled, Optional (plain and encrypted clients) or Required (encrypted clients only). With Optional or Required the server refuses to start without a valid private key. NetPulse:Encryption:PrivateKeyFile empty File with the Base64 private key made by NetPulse.Server keygen. A relative path is resolved against the folder of the server binary. Use this or the variable NETPULSE_SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY, not both. NetPulse:Encryption:PreviousPrivateKeyFiles empty list Retired private keys that are still accepted, so clients that pin an older public key keep working during a rotation. NetPulse:Encryption:PreSharedKey empty Optional Base64 key (32 bytes) that every client must also have. NetPulse:Encryption:PreSharedKeyFile empty Same, read from a file. Set at most one of the two. NetPulse:Encryption:RequireCookie true Make a client echo a cookie before the server does any key agreement. Turn it off only on a private network, it removes the protection against spoofed senders. NetPulse:Encryption:CookieLifetimeMs 30000 How often the cookie secret changes (the previous one is also accepted). At least 1000. NetPulse:Encryption:RekeyAfterPackets 1000000 Replace the sending key after this many packets. 0 turns the packet trigger off. NetPulse:Encryption:RekeyAfterMs 600000 Replace the sending key after this long. 0 turns the time trigger off. NetPulse:Encryption:ReplayWindow 4096 Size of the replay window, in packets. A multiple of 64 from 64 to 65536. NetPulse:Encryption:SessionIdleTimeoutMs 30000 A session with no valid packet for this long is removed and its peer disconnected. At least 1000. NetPulse:Encryption:ReplaceIdleMs 3000 How long a session must be silent before a new handshake from the same address may replace it. NetPulse:Encryption:HandshakeTimeoutMs 5000 How long a half-finished handshake is kept. At least 500. NetPulse:Encryption:PaddingBlock 0 Pad every outgoing record to a multiple of this many bytes. 0 is off, otherwise 16 to 512.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The NetPulse:Security section holds the abuse limits. 0 turns a limit off. The meaning of each key, its default and what happens on a violation are in the table under Security.

Key Default MaxConnectionsPerIp 32 ConnectionAttemptsPerIpPerSecond 20 HandshakesPerIpPerSecond 10 MaxHandshakesPerSecond 2000 AuthDeadlineMs 10000 MaxAuthAttempts 5 MaxMessagesPerSecond / MessageBurst 1000 / 2000 MaxBytesPerSecond / ByteBurst 1048576 / 2097152 MaxMessageBytes 262144 MaxUserIdLength / MaxNickNameLength / MaxAuthTokenLength 128 / 64 / 8192 MaxRoomNameLength 128 MaxPropertiesPerRoom / MaxPropertyBytes 256 / 16384 MaxCachedEventsPerRoom / MaxTargetActors 4096 / 256 RequireRejoinToken false

A negative value stops the server from starting.

docs.title: Console
docs.text: Key Default Effect NetPulse:EnableConsole true Read commands from standard input. Set to false when the process has no console, for example under a service manager.

docs.title: Plugins
Logging
docs.text: Logging uses the standard Logging section and writes single-line messages to the console. The shipped file sets the default level to Information and the Microsoft categories to Warning. To see connection and disconnection messages, set Logging:LogLevel:Default to Debug. See Operations.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft": "Warning"
    }
  },
  "NetPulse": {
    "Port": 5055,
    "ConnectionKey": "NetPulse",
    "MaxConnections": 2000,
    "AppId": "my-game",
    "AppVersionCheck": true,
    "TickRate": 30,
    "DisconnectTimeoutMs": 10000,
    "RoomListIntervalMs": 1000,
    "PeerQueueLimit": 256,
    "RoomQueueCapacity": 4096,
    "OwnershipRequestTimeoutMs": 5000,
    "ShutdownTimeoutMs": 10000,
    "Encryption": {
      "Mode": "Required",
      "PrivateKeyFile": "server.key",
      "PaddingBlock": 0
    },
    "Security": {
      "MaxConnectionsPerIp": 32,
      "MaxMessagesPerSecond": 1000,
      "MaxMessageBytes": 262144,
      "RequireRejoinToken": false
    },
    "EnableConsole": false,
    "Plugins": {
      "Directory": "plugins",
      "Default": "MyPlugin",
      "Auth": "AuthSample",
      "HotReload": true,
      "HookTimeoutMs": 5000,
      "AuthTimeoutMs": 5000,
      "Settings": {
        "AuthSample": {
          "Mode": "Hmac",
          "Secret": "change-me-long-random-string"
        },
        "MyPlugin": {
          "Greeting": "Welcome"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Note

Plugin settings always reach the plugin as strings. Parse numbers and booleans in your factory.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: This page covers building a release folder, the two kinds of build, running the server as a service, and the plugin folder layout.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
dotnet publish src/NetPulse.Server -c Release -o publish
dotnet publish plugins/NetPulse.Plugins.Sample -c Release -o publish/plugins/NetPulse.Plugins.Sample

The first command publishes the server. The second publishes a plugin into the plugins folder inside the output. Publish your own plugins the same way, one folder per plugin.

The publish folder then looks like this:

publish/
  NetPulse.Server.exe        (NetPulse.Server on Linux)
  NetPulse.Server.dll
  NetPulse.Common.dll
  NetPulse.Plugins.dll
  LiteNetLib.dll
  appsettings.json
  plugins/
    NetPulse.Plugins.Sample/
      plugin.json
      NetPulse.Plugins.Sample.dll
      NetPulse.Plugins.Sample.pdb

Edit appsettings.json in the publish folder, or leave it and use environment variables. Remember that the host reads appsettings.json from the working directory, see Running the server.

docs.title: Framework-dependent or self-contained
docs.text:
Framework-dependentSelf-contained 
dotnet publish src/NetPulse.Server -c Release -o publish

About 3 MB. The target machine needs the .NET 10 runtime (Microsoft.NETCore.App). The ASP.NET Core runtime is not required. Runtime updates come from the operating system's package manager.

dotnet publish src/NetPulse.Server -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained -o publish

Use the runtime identifier of the target, for example win-x64, linux-x64 or linux-arm64. The output carries its own runtime and is around 80 MB, and the target machine needs nothing installed. You choose when to update the runtime by publishing again.

Plugins are plain class libraries and load in both modes. Publish them without a runtime identifier; they run on whichever runtime the server uses.

docs.title: Open the port
docs.text:
Clients connect over UDP to NetPulse:Port (5055 by default). Allow inbound UDP on that port, both in the machine's firewall and in any cloud security group or router in front of it. TCP rules do not apply.

Linux (ufw)Linux (firewalld)Windows 
sudo ufw allow 5055/udp

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=5055/udp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "NetPulse" -Direction Inbound -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 5055 -Action Allow

docs.title: Keys for encryption
docs.text:
Create the server key on the machine that runs the server, outside the publish folder if you can, so that a redeploy never overwrites it:

./NetPulse.Server keygen --out /etc/netpulse/server.key

The command prints the public key. Copy it into the Unity settings. Then set the mode and the path, for example with environment variables:

NetPulse__Encryption__Mode=Required
NetPulse__Encryption__PrivateKeyFile=/etc/netpulse/server.key

On Linux the file is created readable by its owner only. On Windows, keep it in a folder that only the service account can read. Alternatively give the key in NETPULSE_SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY (a secret store or the service manager can inject it), and leave PrivateKeyFile empty. The server will not start if both are set, if neither is set, or if the value is not a Base64 key of 32 bytes.

Back the private key up. If you lose it, every client build that pins the matching public key stops working until you ship a new build.

docs.title: Rotating the server key
docs.text:
The public key is compiled into the clients, so a new key has to reach players before the old one stops working. The client can pin several public keys, and the server can accept several private keys. A rotation in three steps:

  1. Run NetPulse.Server keygen --out server-2.key to make the new key.

  2. Ship a client build that lists both public keys (old first or last does not matter, the client tries them in turn). Keep the old key working on the server: make the new file the current key and put the old file into the list of retired keys.

    {
  "NetPulse": {
    "Encryption": {
      "PrivateKeyFile": "server-2.key",
      "PreviousPrivateKeyFiles": [ "server.key" ]
    }
  }
}

  3. When the players have moved to the new build, remove server.key from PreviousPrivateKeyFiles. Builds that still pin only the old key can no longer connect.

The server tells the keys apart by a 4-byte id inside the first handshake message. A client whose key the server does not know gets no reply and reports SecureHandshakeTimeout.

docs.title: Plugin folder layout
docs.text:
The server scans NetPulse:Plugins:Directory (the plugins folder next to the binary by default). Each subfolder is one plugin and needs a plugin.json:

{
  "name": "MyPlugin",
  "assembly": "MyPlugin.dll",
  "factory": "MyNamespace.MyFactory"
}
Field Meaning name The name rooms use in RoomOptions.Plugin, and the key under NetPulse:Plugins:Settings. assembly The dll in the same folder that holds the plugin. factory Full name of a class that implements IPluginFactory. Required for room plugins. auth Full name of a class that implements IAuthPlugin. See Authentication.

A manifest needs name, assembly and at least one of factory or auth. A folder without plugin.json is skipped. The server never loads NetPulse.Plugins.dll, NetPulse.Common.dll, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions.dll or Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions.dll from a plugin folder: it always hands the plugin its own copies. Other dependencies of your plugin load from its folder, so publish the plugin and copy the whole output.

docs.title: Run as a service
docs.text:
The server needs no stdin as a service, so turn the console off: set NetPulse__EnableConsole=false.

Linux (systemd)WindowsContainer

Create /etc/systemd/system/netpulse.service:

[Unit]
Description=NetPulse server
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=netpulse
WorkingDirectory=/opt/netpulse
ExecStart=/opt/netpulse/NetPulse.Server
Environment=NetPulse__EnableConsole=false
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then enable it:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now netpulse
journalctl -u netpulse -f

Make the binary executable (chmod +x /opt/netpulse/NetPulse.Server). For a framework-dependent build, set ExecStart=/usr/bin/dotnet /opt/netpulse/NetPulse.Server.dll. WorkingDirectory matters because appsettings.json is read from there. systemctl stop sends SIGTERM, which starts the graceful shutdown described in Running the server.

The server does not integrate with the Windows service control manager, so registering NetPulse.Server.exe directly with sc.exe does not work. Use a service wrapper such as NSSM:

nssm install NetPulse "C:\NetPulse\NetPulse.Server.exe"
nssm set NetPulse AppDirectory "C:\NetPulse"
nssm set NetPulse AppEnvironmentExtra NetPulse__EnableConsole=false
nssm start NetPulse

A scheduled task that runs at startup with the same working directory also works.

Publish the server, copy the publish folder into an image that has the .NET 10 runtime (or use a self-contained build), and publish the port as UDP:

docker run -p 5055:5055/udp -e NetPulse__EnableConsole=false my-netpulse

Without /udp Docker maps TCP and no client can connect.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
• Plugin only: overwrite the plugin files in place. With HotReload enabled the server loads the new version for new rooms and lets running rooms finish on the old one. See Hot reload.
  • Server binary or configuration: stop the server, replace the files, start it again. Clients in rooms are disconnected from their rooms during the shutdown, so schedule the restart.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: This page covers what you use while the server runs: console commands, metrics, logs and a checklist for common problems.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
The console reads one command per line from standard input while NetPulse:EnableConsole is true.

Command What it does stats Prints uptime, counters, loaded plugins and open rooms. plugins Lists loaded plugins and how many rooms use each. reload <folder> Reloads the plugin in the given subfolder of the plugin directory. Prints reloaded or reload failed. quit or exit Stops the server gracefully.

Anything else prints Unknown command. Available: stats, plugins, reload <folder>, quit.

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
uptime      0.00:12:31
peers       2
rooms       1
msgs in/out 1542 / 3120
bytes in/out 84210 / 160388
plugin errs 0
plugin      NetPulse.Plugins.Sample v1 (rooms: 1)
room        test 2/2 open=True

msgs and bytes count messages the server received and sent since it started. plugin errs counts exceptions thrown by plugin code (see Hooks). Hook timeouts are logged but not counted there. The rooms: 1 after a plugin is the number of rooms currently running on it. The room lines include rooms that are hidden from the lobby list.

docs.title: plugins
docs.text:
NetPulse.Plugins.Sample v1 leases=1

leases is the number of rooms that use this plugin version. During a hot reload the old version stays loaded until its lease count drops to zero.

docs.title: reload
docs.text: reload MyPlugin takes the name of the folder, not the plugin name from plugin.json. If the folder no longer exists, the plugin is unloaded and the command still prints reload failed, because there is nothing to load.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The server publishes its metrics through System.Diagnostics.Metrics under the meter name NetPulse.

Instrument Kind Meaning netpulse.peers gauge Connected peers. netpulse.rooms gauge Rooms that exist. netpulse.msgs_in counter Messages received from clients. netpulse.msgs_out counter Messages sent to clients. netpulse.peers_overloaded counter Peers disconnected for exceeding the queue limits (reason Overloaded). netpulse.ownership_violations counter Network object operations rejected by ownership validation.

Watch them live with the dotnet-counters tool:

dotnet-counters monitor --counters NetPulse --name NetPulse.Server

dotnet-counters and OpenTelemetry collectors can read any Meter. The server ships no exporter of its own; to send these metrics to a monitoring system you add the exporter in your own host code.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The server writes single-line messages to standard output through the standard Logging configuration. There is no log file; capture the output with your service manager (journalctl -u netpulse, a Docker log driver, or a redirect).

info: NetPulse.Lobby[0] Creating room arena for user42
info: NetPulse.Room.arena[0] Room arena closed

The category tells you where a message came from: NetPulse.Lobby, NetPulse.Room.<room name>, NetPulse.Flood, and the class names of the server components. Plugins log through Host.Logger, which uses the room's category.

Messages worth knowing:

Level Message Meaning Warning Disconnecting peer N (room X): exceeded its limit of 256 queued messages A client sent faster than the room could process. See PeerQueueLimit. Warning Queue of room X is full; dropping a message from peer N The room queue hit RoomQueueCapacity. Warning Malformed packet from peer N: ... A packet could not be parsed. Usually a client or protocol mismatch. Warning Rejected object operation from actor N in room X: ... Ownership validation refused a message. Logged at most once a second per actor. Warning Plugin hook P timed out after 00:00:05 in room X A hook exceeded HookTimeoutMs. Error Exception in plugin code of room X A hook, timer or enqueued action threw. Error Plugin hook returned without calling Continue/Fail in room X; treating as Fail A hook finished without making a decision. Warning Plugin hook H was already completed as ...; ignoring ... A hook called Continue, Fail or Cancel twice, or after a timeout. Error Failed to load plugin from F; keeping previous version if any A load or reload failed. The exception follows. Warning Authentication plugin timed out for peer N IAuthPlugin exceeded AuthTimeoutMs. Warning Not all rooms closed within 00:00:10 Shutdown ran out of time.

Connection and disconnection messages are written at Debug level. Set Logging:LogLevel:Default to Debug to see them.

docs.title: Clients cannot connect
docs.text:
• Check that the server logged listening on UDP <port> and that the port matches the client settings.
  • Allow inbound UDP on that port in every firewall and cloud security group. See Deployment.
  • Connection key mismatch: the server silently rejects a client whose key differs from NetPulse:ConnectionKey.
  • NetPulse:MaxConnections reached: new connections are rejected. Compare with netpulse.peers.
  • In Docker, publish the port as 5055:5055/udp.

docs.title: Connecting works but authentication fails
docs.text: Code Cause InvalidAppId (-31) The client's AppId differs from NetPulse:AppId. VersionMismatch (-30) The client speaks another protocol version. Update the package and the server together, or set AppVersionCheck to false to skip the check. AuthenticationFailed (-32) The authentication plugin rejected the client, timed out or failed. The server disconnects the client shortly afterwards. The message says why. NotAuthenticated (-3) The client sent another operation before authenticating.

docs.title: A plugin is not found or fails
docs.text:
• PluginNotFound (-21) with Plugin 'X' is not installed: the room asked for a plugin that is not loaded. The name must equal the name in plugin.json, and the folder must contain that file. The same code with provides no room plugin means the manifest has no factory.
  • No Loaded plugin line at startup: run with Logging:LogLevel:Default at Debug. A folder without plugin.json is logged as skipped.
  • Failed to load plugin from ...: read the exception below it. Typical causes are a wrong assembly or factory name, or a missing dependency in the plugin folder.
  • PluginReportedError (-20) on create or join, with a message such as Plugin hook timed out, Plugin did not respond or Plugin error: the hook failed. The server log has the details. See Hooks.

docs.title: Clients are disconnected with Overloaded
docs.text: A peer sent more than PeerQueueLimit messages that the room had not processed yet. Either the client sends too many messages per second, or the room is slow because a plugin hook waits on I/O. Check netpulse.peers_overloaded and the warning lines above. Fix the slow hook first; raise the limit only if the traffic is legitimate.

docs.title: A room does not close or does not update
docs.text:
• EmptyRoomTtlMs keeps an empty room alive for that long, and PlayerTtlMs keeps a left player inactive. Both are room options set by the client.
  • A plugin that cancels or fails OnBeforeCloseRoomAsync keeps an emptied room open. The server shutdown ignores that and closes it anyway.
  • A hook that never finishes stalls its room until HookTimeoutMs expires. Other rooms keep working.

docs.title: A plugin change has no effect
docs.text: Hot reload waits half a second after the last file change. New rooms get the new version, running rooms keep the old one. If the reload fails, the previous version stays. Run reload <folder> and read the log. See Hot reload.

docs.title: Players drop after about ten seconds
docs.text: A peer that sends nothing is dropped after NetPulse:DisconnectTimeoutMs (10 seconds). On the client this usually means the connection was lost, or the game was paused (for example by a debugger breakpoint) long enough to miss the keep-alive messages.

docs.title: Running the server
docs.text: The server is a .NET 10 console application built on the generic host. It listens on one UDP port, loads plugins from a folder next to the binary and reads console commands from standard input.

docs.title: Run from source
docs.text:
dotnet build
dotnet run --project src/NetPulse.Server

Building the solution also copies the sample plugin (and the AuthSample plugin) into src/NetPulse.Server/bin/<Config>/net10.0/plugins/, which is where the server looks for plugins.

docs.title: Run a published build
docs.text:
After publishing, start the executable or the dll:

./NetPulse.Server
dotnet NetPulse.Server.dll

On Windows the executable is NetPulse.Server.exe.

docs.title: Startup output
docs.text:
A normal start prints one line per loaded plugin, the port and the list of console commands:

info: NetPulse.Server.Plugins.PluginManager[0] Loaded plugin NetPulse.Plugins.Sample v1 from NetPulse.Plugins.Sample
info: NetPulse.Server.Networking.NetPulseServer[0] NetPulse server listening on UDP 5055
info: NetPulse.Server.Commands.ConsoleCommandService[0] Console commands: stats, plugins, reload <folder>, quit

The v1 after the plugin name is a counter that the server increments on every plugin load, so the second plugin that loads shows v2. It is not a version from the plugin itself.

docs.title: Changing settings
docs.text:
The server reads appsettings.json and then overrides it from environment variables and the command line. Later sources win.

appsettings.jsonEnvironment variableCommand line 
{
  "NetPulse": {
    "Port": 6000,
    "AppId": "my-game"
  }
}

NetPulse__Port=6000 ./NetPulse.Server

./NetPulse.Server --NetPulse:Port=6000

Use a double underscore in environment variable names where the key has a colon (NetPulse__Plugins__Auth). Every option is listed in Configuration.

appsettings.json comes from the working directory

The host looks for appsettings.json in the current working directory, not next to the binary. If you start the server from another folder, for example from a service manager, set the working directory to the folder that holds your appsettings.json, or use environment variables. The plugin folder is different: a relative NetPulse:Plugins:Directory is resolved against the folder of the server binary.

Setting NetPulse:Port to 0 picks a random free port. The log line listening on UDP <port> shows which one was chosen.

docs.title: Stopping the server
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C, type quit (or exit) in the console, or send SIGTERM. The server then:

  1. Stops accepting new connections.
  2. Closes every room, running OnBeforeCloseRoomAsync and OnCloseRoomAsync for each, within NetPulse:ShutdownTimeoutMs (10 seconds by default). If rooms do not finish in time, the server logs Not all rooms closed within ... and continues.
  3. Stops the network manager, disposes the plugins and unloads their load contexts.

Clients in a room receive an ErrorInfo event with the code RoomClosed before they are disconnected.

docs.title: When the server refuses to start
docs.text:
The process exits with an unhandled exception in two cases:

  • The UDP port is already in use: Could not bind UDP port 5055.
  • NetPulse:Plugins:Auth names a plugin that is not installed, or that fails to load or to construct: Plugins:Auth is set to '...' but no authentication plugin could be loaded; refusing to start without authentication.

The second case is deliberate. A server that was configured to authenticate never falls back to accepting everyone. See Security.

docs.title: Console input
docs.text: The console reads commands while NetPulse:EnableConsole is true. If standard input is closed or redirected from /dev/null, the console service simply ends and the server keeps running. Set the option to false for services and containers. The commands are described in Operations.

docs.title: Try it with the test client
docs.text:
The repository includes a bot client, tools/NetPulse.TestClient:

dotnet run --project tools/NetPulse.TestClient -- --bots 2 --room test --seconds 6
Flag Default Meaning --host 127.0.0.1 Server address --port 5055 Server UDP port --bots 2 Number of bot clients --room test Room name --plugin NetPulse.Plugins.Sample Plugin requested for the room; pass an empty string for none --seconds 6 How long the bots exchange events --app-id none AppId sent to the server --key NetPulse LiteNetLib connection key --token none Authentication token --make-token, --secret, --user, --nick, --ttl-minutes Print an AuthSample token instead of running bots, see Authentication

Exit code 0 means the bots saw each other's events, the sample plugin's timer ticks and a server-side score, and that the sample plugin rejected event 99. The last check always runs, so with --plugin "" or a plugin other than the sample the client reports FAILED even when the server works. In that case read the joined lines instead: they show that connect, authenticate and join succeeded.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The server treats every client as untrusted. This page lists what it checks on its own, what transport encryption gives you, and where you have to add checks yourself.

docs.title: What is protected and what is not
docs.text:
Version 0.4 can encrypt and authenticate the whole UDP stream between a Unity client and the server. It defends against:

  • eavesdropping: an observer on the network sees no AppId, token, room name or game data;
  • forged, modified and replayed packets, including the LiteNetLib acknowledgements and disconnect messages;
  • a man in the middle, because the client pins the server's public key;
  • hijacking a session from the same address and spoofed senders used to amplify traffic;
  • exhausting the server's CPU, memory and connection slots before a client has proven an address;
  • abuse by a client that has connected, through per-peer rate limits and size limits.

It does not protect you from the player. The client runs on the attacker's machine:

  • The process memory, the session keys and the game logic are all readable and editable there. Encryption stops other people from reading or changing the traffic, it does not stop the player from sending whatever they like through a legitimate, encrypted connection.
  • Everything that decides fairness must be checked by the server or a plugin. Treat every value from a client as untrusted, encrypted or not.
  • Secrets that ship in the build (ConnectionKey, AppId, the pre-shared key) can be extracted. Obfuscation does not change that and NetPulse does not claim it as protection. The server public key is not a secret, but it must be the real one: it is what stops a man in the middle.
  • The transport does not authenticate the player. Any client that knows the server public key can complete the handshake. Use an authentication plugin to know who the player is.
  • Not covered in 0.4: anti-cheat, build attestation, a connection that survives a change of the client's address (NAT rebinding drops the connection, as before), mutual authentication with a client key, and post-quantum key exchange.

docs.title: Connection key, AppId and version
docs.text:
Three values gate who can talk to the server:

  • The connection key (NetPulse:ConnectionKey) is checked by the transport. A client with another key never gets a connection.
  • The AppId (NetPulse:AppId) is checked when the client authenticates. If you set it, a client that sends another value gets InvalidAppId.
  • The protocol version is checked at the same time when NetPulse:AppVersionCheck is true. A mismatch returns VersionMismatch.

All three ship inside your game, so anyone who unpacks the build can read them. They keep unrelated clients and outdated builds out. They do not prove that a client is a legitimate player. With encryption on, they no longer travel in clear text.

A client that fails the AppId or version check stays connected but unauthenticated, and the server answers every other operation with NotAuthenticated.

docs.title: Transport encryption
docs.text:
NetPulse:Encryption:Mode selects what the server accepts:

Mode Behaviour Disabled (default) No encryption layer is installed. The wire format and the per-packet overhead are exactly as in version 0.3. Optional Encrypted and plain clients both connect. A plain packet from an address that already has an encrypted session is dropped, so a plain packet cannot be injected into an encrypted connection. Required Only encrypted clients connect. Every plain datagram is dropped without a reply.

Optional exists for a migration. It cannot protect a client that connects in plain text, and it lets an attacker force a downgrade of a client that is willing to use plain text. The Unity client has no "prefer encryption" mode for that reason: it is either Off or Required, and a Required client never sends or accepts a plain packet. Use Required in production.

With Optional or Required the server refuses to start unless it has a valid private key.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
There is one fixed set of algorithms on every platform and nothing is negotiated, so a downgrade attack has nothing to downgrade:

  • key agreement X25519, authenticated with the server's static key through the Noise pattern NK (Noise_NK_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256, or Noise_NKpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 when a pre-shared key is set). It gives server authentication and forward secrecy;
  • records protected with ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439), one key per direction;
  • SHA-256 and HKDF for key derivation.

X25519 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are implemented in managed code in NetPulse.Common, because the .NET versions of these ciphers are not available in Unity's Mono and IL2CPP. They run in constant time, without secret-dependent branches or table lookups, and without allocating memory per packet. They are checked against the RFC 7748 and RFC 8439 test vectors and against independent implementations. SHA-256, HMAC and the random number generator come from the platform.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Create the server key once:

NetPulse.Server keygen --out server.key

The command writes the private key to the file (it refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you add --force) and prints the public key as Base64. Put the public key in the Unity settings (Connecting). Point the server at the private key:

{
  "NetPulse": {
    "Encryption": {
      "Mode": "Required",
      "PrivateKeyFile": "server.key"
    }
  }
}

Or give the key in the environment variable NETPULSE_SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY. Configure only one of the two. The private key is never part of appsettings.json, is never logged, and is not echoed in error messages. Keep the file out of version control and readable only by the account that runs the server. A relative path is resolved against the folder of the server binary.

The server fails closed. It refuses to start when the mode is Optional or Required and the key is missing, malformed, or configured twice, and when a numeric option is out of range. Rotating the key is described in Deployment.

docs.title: Pre-shared key
docs.text: NetPulse:Encryption:PreSharedKey (Base64, 32 bytes) or PreSharedKeyFile adds a second secret to the handshake. A client without the same value cannot finish it. The value must also be in the client build, so anyone who extracts it can use it: it only filters out clients that do not carry your build. A server with a pre-shared key accepts only clients that use one.

docs.title: How a connection starts
docs.text:
1. The client sends an Init record with the key id, a Noise message and padding, in place of the first LiteNetLib connect request.
  2. The server answers with a short Retry that carries a cookie, the HMAC of the sender's address and port. It does no key agreement yet and keeps no state. The reply is always shorter than the request, so the server cannot be used to amplify traffic towards a spoofed address.
  3. The client repeats Init with the cookie. Only now does the server do the key agreement, and it replies with the second Noise message. A repeated Init with the same ephemeral key gets the cached reply without new work.
