  4. The client sends its LiteNetLib connect request inside the first encrypted record. The server activates the session when it receives the first valid record.

Failures are silent. A wrong server key, wrong pre-shared key, damaged message or unknown key id gets no reply and increments a metric, so the server gives an attacker no oracle. The client sees SecureHandshakeTimeout. The cookie secret rotates every CookieLifetimeMs, and the current and previous secrets are accepted.

docs.title: Records, replay and rekeying
docs.text:
After the handshake every datagram is a record of 26 bytes of overhead: type, key epoch, an 8-byte counter, the encrypted payload and a 16-byte tag. The whole LiteNetLib packet is inside, including its headers, acknowledgements and disconnect messages. The counter only grows and a sliding window (ReplayWindow, 4096 by default) rejects duplicates and very old packets. The window moves only after the tag has been verified, so a forged packet cannot move it. A modified byte anywhere in a record fails verification. When the counter approaches its limit, the session is closed.

Each direction replaces its key independently, after RekeyAfterPackets packets (1,000,000) or RekeyAfterMs (10 minutes), by hashing the old key. Packets that were lost or arrive late still decrypt, and the old key is erased when the replay window has moved past it.

PaddingBlock (0 by default, which is off) pads every record to a multiple of the block size, which hides the length of messages from an observer at the cost of bandwidth. It reduces the usable packet size by up to the block size. Use the same value on the client and the server.

docs.title: Sessions and address hijacking
docs.text: Sessions are stored per address and port. A new handshake from an address that has a working session is ignored unless that session has been silent for ReplaceIdleMs (3 seconds). Replacing a session always disconnects the LiteNetLib peer bound to the old session first, so a new session never inherits an authenticated peer: whoever takes over an address has to authenticate again. A session is removed when its peer disconnects (after a second, so the last packets can leave) or after SessionIdleTimeoutMs without traffic.

docs.title: What the plugins see
docs.text: AuthRequest.IsEncrypted and AuthRequest.ChannelBinding are passed to the authentication plugin. The channel binding is the Noise handshake hash, 32 bytes that are unique to this connection. A token that contains it is valid only on that connection and cannot be replayed on another. IActor.IsEncrypted tells room plugins whether a player's connection is encrypted.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Metric Meaning netpulse.handshakes_ok Sessions that were activated netpulse.handshakes_failed Handshakes that failed verification or used an unknown key netpulse.handshakes_rate_limited Handshakes dropped by the per-address limit, the server budget or a busy session netpulse.cookies_sent Retry replies sent netpulse.decrypt_failures Records that failed verification netpulse.replays Valid records that were seen before netpulse.rekeys Key replacements, both directions netpulse.plaintext_rejected Plain datagrams dropped in Required mode, or from an encrypted address

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• A datagram that the layer drops does not go through LiteNetLib's normal path, and LiteNetLib 1.3.5 does not return its buffer to its pool in that case. A flood of garbage costs allocations on the receive thread. Stop a volumetric flood in the firewall or upstream.
  • An outgoing packet that the layer cannot encrypt, for example for an address whose session has already gone, is dropped by sending an empty datagram.
  • One key agreement costs about 1 ms of CPU in managed code (three X25519 operations of about 0.3 ms each), so one core completes about 1000 handshakes per second. MaxHandshakesPerSecond bounds the total; its default of 2000 is a ceiling for the whole machine, not a promise. Encrypting and decrypting a 1000-byte record costs about 12 microseconds together.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Without an authentication plugin the server accepts every client that passes the checks above. The UserId and NickName the client sends become its identity. Two consequences follow:

  • A client can claim any UserId. If you use PlayerTtlMs so that players can rejoin, another client that sends the same UserId takes over the inactive player's slot, unless you turn on NetPulse:Security:RequireRejoinToken (see below).
  • A nickname is only a label. Do not use it for permissions.

To authenticate players, install a plugin that implements IAuthPlugin and set NetPulse:Plugins:Auth to its name. The server then uses the UserId and NickName the plugin returns and ignores the client's. The repository ships AuthSample, which verifies HMAC-signed tokens or asks your HTTP service. See Authentication.

The server fails closed:

  • If NetPulse:Plugins:Auth is set and the plugin is missing, throws while loading, or does not provide an IAuthPlugin, the server refuses to start.
  • If the plugin throws while checking a client, the client gets AuthenticationFailed.
  • A rejected client, or one that exceeds AuthTimeoutMs, gets AuthenticationFailed and is disconnected about a quarter of a second later.

Authentication tokens are never written to the log. With encryption off they still cross the network in clear text, so use short-lived tokens, such as the AuthSample HMAC tokens with a short TTL, and never send a password as the token.

docs.title: Limits for connected clients
docs.text:
NetPulse:Security holds the limits. A value of 0 turns a limit off. The defaults are chosen so that normal play never hits them. Violating a limit counts in a metric, and the request is refused or the peer is disconnected as shown.

Key Default When it is exceeded MaxConnectionsPerIp 32 A further connection from the address is rejected. Players behind one NAT share the limit. ConnectionAttemptsPerIpPerSecond 20 Connection requests above the rate (a burst of twice that is allowed) are rejected. HandshakesPerIpPerSecond 10 Encryption handshakes above the rate are dropped after the cookie check. Encryption only. MaxHandshakesPerSecond 2000 Server-wide budget for key agreement. Encryption only. AuthDeadlineMs 10000 A peer that has not authenticated in time is disconnected with AuthTimeout. MaxAuthAttempts 5 More than this many authenticate requests without success disconnect the peer with TooManyAuthAttempts. MaxMessagesPerSecond / MessageBurst 1000 / 2000 Token bucket per peer. The peer is disconnected with RateLimited. MaxBytesPerSecond / ByteBurst 1048576 / 2097152 Token bucket per peer, counted in message bytes. Disconnected with RateLimited. MaxMessageBytes 262144 A larger message disconnects the peer with RateLimited. MaxUserIdLength 128 InvalidRequest. MaxNickNameLength 64 InvalidRequest. MaxAuthTokenLength 8192 InvalidRequest. MaxRoomNameLength 128 InvalidRequest. MaxPropertiesPerRoom 256 InvalidRequest when a property update or the creation options would exceed it. MaxPropertyBytes 16384 InvalidRequest when one serialized property value is larger. MaxCachedEventsPerRoom 4096 InvalidRequest for an event that would be cached beyond the limit. MaxTargetActors 256 InvalidRequest for an event addressed to more actors. RequireRejoinToken false See below.

The server refuses a request that exceeds a limit instead of cutting it down. UserId, NickName and room names must not contain control characters. Text from a client is cleaned of control characters before it is written to the log, so a client cannot forge log lines.

The reader that parses incoming messages checks every declared length against the bytes that are really there before it allocates, and it limits the number of nested containers in one message to 4096, so a small packet cannot make the server build a huge object graph.

docs.title: Rejoin tokens
docs.text: With PlayerTtlMs a player who loses the connection keeps the seat for a while and can return with the same UserId. Without an authentication plugin that UserId is only what the client claims. With RequireRejoinToken set to true, the server gives each player a random token when they join a room, replaces it on every join, and the Unity client presents it when it returns to the same room. A client that has no valid token for the seat gets Forbidden. The token lives in the client's memory, so a player who restarts the game does not return to the seat.

docs.title: Flood protection
docs.text:
Each peer may have at most NetPulse:PeerQueueLimit messages (256 by default) queued and not yet processed. The count covers the lobby and the room together. When a peer exceeds it, the server drops the message and disconnects the peer with the reason Overloaded. The netpulse.peers_overloaded metric counts these.

A second bound, NetPulse:RoomQueueCapacity (4096), caps the messages waiting in one room or in the lobby. When it is full, the message is dropped and the peer with the most queued messages is disconnected, which may be a different peer than the sender. Server-internal work, such as timers and Host.Enqueue, does not count against either limit.

What this does and does not cover:

  • It limits work waiting in a queue, so a client that floods a slow room is removed before it can grow the queue without bound.
  • The rate and size limits above cover messages and bytes per second.
  • Keep-alive pings and authentication requests bypass the queues, and the rate limits still count them.
  • NetPulse:MaxConnections caps the number of connected peers, and the per-address limits above cap what one address can take. A flood of packets that never connect has to be stopped by the firewall.

docs.title: Ownership validation
docs.text:
The server keeps a registry of network objects in every room and checks each message that touches one. A rejected message is dropped, the sender gets Forbidden (or an ErrorInfo event if the request had no request id, at most once a second), the server logs a rate-limited warning, and netpulse.ownership_violations counts it. Nobody is disconnected for this.

Message Accepted when Object instantiate (event 240) The view id is at least 1000, belongs to the sender (viewId / 1000 == actorId) and is not in use. Object destroy (event 241) The sender owns the object, or is the master client. Scene objects cannot be destroyed. State sync (event 243) The sender is the current owner. Master sync variable set (event 245) The sender is the master client. Transfer ownership The object's mode allows it: Fixed never changes; Takeover lets anyone take it; the owner or the master can assign to anyone; Request lets only the owner or the master assign. Register scene objects The sender is the master client. RPC (event 242) and messages (event 244) Always accepted. Validate them in a plugin if they matter.

Scene objects (view ids 1 to 999) belong to the master client until the master assigns them to someone. When a player leaves for good, it loses the objects it currently owns; its scene objects return to the master. An inactive player (waiting to rejoin) keeps everything.

A plugin can add its own veto with OnBeforeTransferOwnershipAsync, see Hooks.

docs.title: Reserved events
docs.text:
A client may raise event codes 0 to 199 (your own events) and the object events 240 to 245: instantiate, destroy, RPC, state sync, message and master sync variable. Any other code is reserved for the server and the request fails with Forbidden and the message Reserved event code. The server events that clients receive include the room list, join and leave notices, property changes, master and ownership changes, and ErrorInfo. The complete list is in Codes and keys.

Plugins are not bound by this rule: Host.BroadcastEvent can send any code.

docs.title: Reserved properties
docs.text:
Four room property keys control the room itself, so only the master client may change them:

Key Controls _isOpen Whether new players may join. _isVisible Whether the room appears in the lobby list. _maxPlayers The player limit, clamped to 0 to 255. _scene The current network scene. A change removes scene-bound objects.

A non-master client that includes one of these keys in a room property update gets Forbidden and nothing is applied. Only the master client may change another player's properties; everyone may change their own. A plugin can change reserved keys through Host.SetRoomProperties, which skips these checks.

Every other room property can be written by any client in the room. Do not keep authoritative values such as scores or inventories there unless you guard them. The easiest guard is a plugin:

ProtectedKeysPlugin.cs
using NetPulse.Plugins;

namespace ProtectedKeys;

public sealed class ProtectedKeysPlugin : RoomPlugin
{
    private const string ServerPrefix = "server_";

    public ProtectedKeysPlugin(IPluginHost host)
        : base(host)
    {
    }

    public override ValueTask OnBeforeSetPropertiesAsync(IBeforeSetPropertiesCallInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        foreach (var key in info.Properties.Keys)
        {
            if (key.StartsWith(ServerPrefix, StringComparison.Ordinal))
            {
                info.Fail($"Property '{key}' is read only");
                return default;
            }
        }

        info.Continue();
        return default;
    }
}

The plugin writes server_* keys itself with Host.SetRoomProperties, which does not go through the hook.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Generate a server key, set NetPulse:Encryption:Mode to Required, and put the public key into the Unity settings.
  2. Set NetPulse:AppId and keep AppVersionCheck on.
  3. Configure an authentication plugin and short-lived tokens. Bind them to ChannelBinding if you can.
  4. Put authoritative state behind a plugin and validate events in OnRaiseEventAsync.
  5. Keep the default limits unless you measured a reason to change them, and watch netpulse.peers_overloaded, netpulse.peers_rate_limited, netpulse.ownership_violations and netpulse.decrypt_failures.
  6. Open only the UDP port, and restrict it with a firewall where you can.

docs.title: Analyzers
docs.text:
The package ships a Roslyn source generator and analyzers in one DLL, Runtime/Analyzers/NetPulse.Generators.dll. Unity applies it to NetPulse.Runtime and to every assembly that references it. The generator writes the serialization and dispatch code for [NetRpc], SyncVar<T>, [NetSerializable] and INetMessage. The analyzers check your code against the rules that make that possible and report problems as compiler diagnostics with the ids NP0001 to NP0011. They show up in the Unity console and in any IDE that loads Roslyn analyzers.

Id Severity Rule NP0001 Error A class with [NetRpc], SyncVar<T> or [NetSerializable] is not partial NP0002 Error [NetRpc] outside a NetworkBehaviour NP0003 Error Unsupported RPC parameter type NP0004 Error An RPC returns a value or has ref, out or in parameters NP0005 Error RPC overload NP0006 Error Unsupported member in a [NetSerializable] or INetMessage type NP0007 Error SyncVar<T> with an unsupported T NP0008 Warning A SyncVar<T> field is not readonly or is outside a NetworkBehaviour NP0009 Error Id collision (RPCs in a type, messages and serializable types in an assembly) NP0010 Error [Synced] on an unsupported field type NP0011 Warning CallRpc("Name", ...) while a [NetRpc] method with that name exists

The examples below show the smallest code that triggers each rule, followed by a fix. Types the generator handles are partial, and sealed partial is fine.

docs.title: NP0001: type must be partial
docs.text:
The generator adds members to your class from a second file, which only works if the class is declared partial. The same applies to a type that contains such a class.

NP0001
using NetPulse;

public sealed class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(int damage)
    {
    }
}

Add partial:

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(int damage)
    {
    }
}

docs.title: NP0002: [NetRpc] outside a NetworkBehaviour
docs.text:
RPCs belong to network objects, so the class has to derive from NetworkBehaviour.

NP0002
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed partial class Helper : MonoBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Ping()
    {
    }
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Helper : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Ping()
    {
    }
}

docs.title: NP0003: unsupported RPC parameter type
docs.text:
Parameters use the types listed under serializable types. A GameObject is not one of them.

NP0003
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed partial class Spawner : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Spawn(GameObject prefab)
    {
    }
}

Send a NetworkObject, or pass an id and look the object up on the receiving side.

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Spawner : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Spawn(NetworkObject target)
    {
    }
}

NetRpcInfo is allowed only as the last parameter. Putting it elsewhere also reports NP0003.

docs.title: NP0004: invalid RPC signature
docs.text:
An RPC is a one-way call. It must return void and take its parameters by value.

NP0004
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private int Hit(int damage) => damage;
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(int damage)
    {
    }
}

If the caller needs an answer, make the answer another RPC that goes back to the sender (Rpc.To(info.Sender)).

docs.title: NP0005: RPC overload
docs.text:
The id of an RPC is a hash of its method name, so two methods with one name cannot be told apart.

NP0005
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(int damage)
    {
    }

    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(float damage)
    {
    }
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void Hit(int damage)
    {
    }

    [NetRpc]
    private void HitFloat(float damage)
    {
    }
}

docs.title: NP0006: unsupported member in a serializable type
docs.text:
Public fields and auto-properties of a [NetSerializable] or INetMessage type must use supported types. Generic types are not supported, and a class needs a parameterless constructor.

NP0006
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

[NetSerializable]
public partial struct Loadout
{
    public GameObject Prefab;
    public int Slot;
}

using NetPulse;

[NetSerializable]
public partial struct Loadout
{
    public NetworkObject Prefab;
    public int Slot;
}

docs.title: NP0007: unsupported SyncVar type
docs.text:
SyncVar<T> accepts the same types as messages. Mark a custom type [NetSerializable] to use it.

NP0007
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed partial class Turret : NetworkBehaviour
{
    private readonly SyncVar<GameObject> _target = new();
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Turret : NetworkBehaviour
{
    private readonly SyncVar<NetworkObject> _target = new();
}

docs.title: NP0008: SyncVar field shape
docs.text:
A SyncVar<T> field should be readonly, because replacing the field would detach it from the network. A field outside a NetworkBehaviour is never synchronized. This is a warning.

NP0008
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    private SyncVar<int> _health = new(100);
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    private readonly SyncVar<int> _health = new(100);
}

docs.title: NP0009: id collision
docs.text:
Ids are 16-bit hashes of names, so two different names can share an id. The analyzer reports it when two RPCs in one class collide, and when two message or [NetSerializable] types in one assembly collide. Rename one of them.

NP0009
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Lamp : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void SendTarget(int id)
    {
    }

    [NetRpc]
    private void ResetLight(int id)
    {
    }
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Lamp : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void SendTarget(int id)
    {
    }

    [NetRpc]
    private void ResetLamp(int id)
    {
    }
}

The example is real: both names hash to the same id. Collisions are rare, and when one occurs the diagnostic names both members and the shared id.

docs.title: NP0010: unsupported [Synced] field
docs.text:
[Synced] fields support only primitives, string, a few Unity structs and enums (see state sync). Use SyncVar<T> for other types.

NP0010
using System.Collections.Generic;
using NetPulse;

public sealed class Backpack : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [Synced] private List<int> _slots = new();
}

using System;
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Backpack : NetworkBehaviour
{
    private readonly SyncVar<int[]> _slots = new(Array.Empty<int>());
}

docs.title: NP0011: use the generated Rpc API
docs.text:
CallRpc("Name", ...) with a literal name still works but uses reflection and is not type-checked. When a valid [NetRpc] method with that name exists, the analyzer suggests Rpc.Name(...). This is a warning.

NP0011
using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
    }

    public void Damage(int amount) => CallRpc("TakeDamage", RpcTarget.All, amount);
}

using NetPulse;

public sealed partial class Hero : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [NetRpc]
    private void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
    }

    public void Damage(int amount) => Rpc.TakeDamage(amount);
}

The old call stays valid when you build the name at runtime, which the analyzer cannot see (low-level API).

docs.title: Async
docs.text:
Every request that takes time returns a NetOperation (or NetOperation<T> when it has a result). One operation type works with await, with coroutines and with callbacks. It needs no Awaitable, so it runs the same on Unity 2021.3 and Unity 6.

using System.Collections;
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class OperationStyles : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void AsAwait()
    {
        var room = await Pulse.JoinOrCreateRoom("arena");
        Debug.Log($"Joined {room.Name}");
    }

    private IEnumerator AsCoroutine()
    {
        var operation = Pulse.JoinOrCreateRoom("arena");
        yield return operation;
        Debug.Log(operation.IsSuccess ? operation.Result.Name : operation.Error.ToString());
    }

    private void AsCallback()
    {
        Pulse.JoinOrCreateRoom("arena").Completed += operation => Debug.Log(operation.IsSuccess ? "ok" : operation.Error.ToString());
    }
}

docs.title: The operation object
docs.text:
Member Meaning IsDone The operation finished, successfully or not IsSuccess Done, with no error and not canceled HasError, Error A failure. Error is a NetError with ReturnCode and Message. IsCanceled Cancel() was called before it finished Result The value of a NetOperation<T>, valid after success Completed An event raised when the operation finishes. If it already finished, a new subscriber is called at once. Cancel() Stops waiting, see below

NetOperation is a CustomYieldInstruction, so yield return operation waits for it without extra code. The continuation of an await and the Completed handlers run on the main thread, in the NetPulse update, so you can use Unity objects freely.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• await throws NetPulseException for a failed operation. It carries ReturnCode and the message. See codes and keys for server codes and connecting for the client-side ones (Timeout, Disconnected, InvalidState).
  • In a coroutine or callback, check HasError and Error. Nothing is thrown.
  • An exception thrown by a Completed handler is logged and does not affect the other handlers.
  • Wrap await in try/catch inside an async void method. Otherwise an exception reaches Unity's log without any context.
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class SafeJoin : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        try
        {
            await Pulse.Connect();
            await Pulse.JoinRoom("arena");
        }
        catch (NetPulseException e)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning($"Failed with {e.ReturnCode}: {e.Message}");
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Cancelling
docs.text:
operation.Cancel() completes the operation at once with IsCanceled set. Awaiting a canceled operation throws OperationCanceledException. For waits that live only on the client (WaitForPlayersAsync and WaitUntilAsync), Cancel() removes the wait. For requests that were already sent to the server, such as Connect(), JoinRoom() or the ownership calls, it only stops you from waiting: the request still reaches the server and takes effect there.

using System;
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class WaitForOpponents : MonoBehaviour
{
    private NetOperation _waiting;

    public async void Begin()
    {
        _waiting = Pulse.WaitForPlayersAsync(2);

        try
        {
            await _waiting;
            Debug.Log("Opponent found");
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            Debug.Log("Stopped waiting");
        }
    }

    public void Stop() => _waiting?.Cancel();
}

docs.title: Waiting helpers
Your own operations
docs.text: NetOperation.Succeeded(), NetOperation.Failed(code, message), NetOperation<T>.Succeeded(result) and NetOperation<T>.Failed(code, message) create finished operations. They are useful when a method of your own has to return the same kind of object as NetPulse calls, for example in tests or when a precondition fails early.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Three ready-made components cover the common cases: NetworkTransform, NetworkRigidbody and NetworkAnimator. Each one is a NetworkBehaviour, so the GameObject also needs a NetworkObject on its root. They are found under Add Component > NetPulse. All of them send state from the owner and apply it on everyone else, using OnSerialize underneath (state sync).

docs.title: NetworkTransform
docs.text:
Synchronizes position, rotation and scale, and smooths the motion on remote clients by interpolation. Only one per object.

Sync:

Option Default Meaning Sync Position on Send and apply the position Sync Rotation on Send and apply the rotation Sync Scale off Send and apply the local scale Use Local Space on Use localPosition and localRotation. Turn it off to sync world space. For a root object both are the same. Reliable off Off sends with UnreliableSequenced: old packets are dropped and a loss does not stall anything. On sends ReliableOrdered.

Send thresholds (owner side):

Option Default Meaning Position Threshold 0.001 A move smaller than this distance is not sent. It also applies to scale. Rotation Threshold 0.1 A rotation smaller than this angle in degrees is not sent

Receive (other clients):

Option Default Meaning Interpolation Delay 0 Seconds to render in the past. 0 means automatic, see below. Extrapolate off When no newer snapshot has arrived, keep moving along the last velocity Max Extrapolation Time 0.25 Longest extrapolation in seconds Teleport Distance 0 If the gap between the current and the target position exceeds this, the object snaps to the target and the buffer is cleared. 0 disables the check.

Remote clients keep a buffer of timestamped snapshots and show the object at ServerTime - delay, blending between the two snapshots around that time. Snapshots that are older than the last one are discarded. After an ownership change the buffer is cleared.

The automatic delay is two state send intervals. The interval comes from Send Rate, Serialization Rate and the server tick rate, the same way the object is actually sent (ticks and time). With the defaults (Send Rate 20, Serialization Rate 0, a 30 Hz server tick) an object is sent every 2 ticks, so the delay is about 0.13 s. Set Interpolation Delay yourself only if you want a different trade-off between smoothness and lag.

docs.title: NetworkRigidbody
docs.text:
Synchronizes a Rigidbody and requires one on the same object. It always uses UnreliableSequenced delivery.

Option Default Meaning Sync Velocity on Also send linear and angular velocity, which improves extrapolation Interpolation Delay 0 Seconds to render in the past. 0 means automatic, the same two send intervals as NetworkTransform. Teleport Distance 5 A gap larger than this snaps the body to the target. 0 disables it.

On the owner the body behaves normally. On other clients NetPulse makes it kinematic (clearing its velocity first) and moves it with MovePosition and MoveRotation in FixedUpdate, extrapolating up to a quarter of a second when snapshots run late. When ownership changes, the new owner gets back the Is Kinematic value the prefab had, and the old owner turns kinematic. Pair the component with a Takeover or Request ownership mode if players should be able to pick the object up and throw it.

Use either NetworkTransform or NetworkRigidbody to move an object, not both.

docs.title: NetworkAnimator
docs.text:
Synchronizes the parameters of an Animator, so remote copies play the same transitions.

Option Default Meaning Animator auto The Animator to sync. If empty, the component on the same GameObject is used. Sync Layer Weights off Also sync the weights of layers 1 and up
  • bool, int and float parameters are streamed with the object's state. The owner reads them and everyone else sets them.
  • Triggers are not part of the stream. Call networkAnimator.SetTrigger("Attack") on the owner. It fires the trigger locally and sends an RPC that fires it on every other client. Calls from a non-owner are ignored. ResetTrigger is local only.
  • The parameter list is read from the controller in Awake, so assign the controller before the object is created.
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class AttackAnimation : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private NetworkAnimator _networkAnimator;
    [SerializeField] private Animator _animator;

    public void Attack(float speed)
    {
        _animator.SetFloat("Speed", speed);
        _networkAnimator.SetTrigger("Attack");
    }
}

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text: For other cases, write a NetworkBehaviour with SyncVar<T> or OnSerialize (state sync). The three components above are ordinary scripts of that kind, and reading NetworkTransform is a good starting point for a custom interpolator.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Pulse is the static entry point of the client. (It is not called NetPulse because NetPulse is also the namespace, and C# cannot have a type and a namespace with the same name visible from user code.) Connecting takes one call, and the call returns an operation you can await.

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectOnStart : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        Pulse.NickName = "Alice";
        Pulse.StateChanged += state => Debug.Log($"State: {state}");

        try
        {
            await Pulse.Connect();
            Debug.Log($"Connected as {Pulse.UserId}, ping {Pulse.RoundTripTimeMs} ms");
        }
        catch (NetPulseException e)
        {
            Debug.LogError($"Connect failed ({e.ReturnCode}): {e.Message}");
        }
    }
}

Pulse.Connect() reads NetPulseSettings (see settings and editor), opens the UDP connection and authenticates. It completes when the state reaches Connected. If you do not set Pulse.NickName, the client uses the Default Nick Name from the settings, and Player followed by a random number if that is empty too.

The operation can also be used from a coroutine or with a callback. The async page covers NetOperation in full.

using System.Collections;
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectInCoroutine : MonoBehaviour
{
    private IEnumerator Start()
    {
        var operation = Pulse.Connect();
        yield return operation;

        if (operation.HasError)
        {
            Debug.LogError(operation.Error.ToString());
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text:
Pulse.Connect() uses the settings asset in Resources. Pass your own NetPulseSettings to override it for this and later calls:

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectWithSettings : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        var settings = ScriptableObject.CreateInstance<NetPulseSettings>();
        settings.Host = "game.example.com";
        settings.Port = 5055;
        settings.AppId = "my-game";
        settings.AppVersion = "1.2";
        await Pulse.Connect(settings);
    }
}

Pulse.Connect(settings) also becomes the active NetPulseSettings.Instance, so rates, the prefab registry and the other fields come from it. A third overload takes a ConnectionOptions object with Host, Port, ConnectionKey, AppId, AppVersion, UserId, NickName, AuthToken, RequestTimeout and the encryption fields. It skips the settings asset entirely, which suits tests and tools:

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectWithOptions : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        var options = new ConnectionOptions
        {
            Host = "127.0.0.1",
            Port = 5055,
            AppId = "my-game",
            AppVersion = "1.2",
            NickName = "Bot"
        };
        await Pulse.Connect(options);
    }
}

ConnectionKey is a shared secret that the UDP handshake checks. It defaults to NetPulse and must equal the key the server is configured with.

The settings can also turn on Run In Background: when it is on, Pulse.Connect sets Application.runInBackground so the connection survives a lost window focus. It never switches the option off.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: The client sends a UserId with the handshake. By default it is a random id generated once and kept in PlayerPrefs under NetPulse.UserId, so the same install is recognized across sessions. With Persist User Id off, every Connect uses a fresh id. When an authentication plugin is active, the server's answer decides the final UserId and NickName, and the client adopts them (Pulse.UserId, Pulse.Client.NickName).

docs.title: Authentication token
docs.text:
By default the server accepts any client. If it runs an authentication plugin (see authentication), pass the token before connecting:

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectWithToken : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private string _token;

    private async void Start()
    {
        Pulse.AuthToken = _token;
        await Pulse.Connect();
    }
}

A rejected token fails the Connect operation with AuthenticationFailed (-32), and the server drops the connection. The token is cleared when the domain reloads or play mode restarts, so set it on every run.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
NetPulse can encrypt and authenticate the whole connection. The server decides what it accepts (Security), the client decides what it sends:

Client mode Behaviour Off (default) The client sends plain packets. It connects to a server whose mode is Disabled or Optional. Required The client never sends and never accepts a plain packet. It connects to a server whose mode is Optional or Required.

There is no "prefer encryption" mode on purpose: a client that falls back to plain text can be pushed into it by an attacker.

To turn it on:

  1. Run NetPulse.Server keygen on the server. It prints the public key. The private key stays on the server.
  2. Open Project Settings > NetPulse (or the settings asset) and set Encryption Mode to Required.
  3. Paste the public key into Server Public Keys. The field checks the format. Add a second key only while you rotate the server key (Deployment).
  4. Optionally fill Pre Shared Key if the server uses one.

The same fields exist in code:

using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common.Security;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class ConnectEncrypted : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private string _serverPublicKey = string.Empty;

    private async void Start()
    {
        var options = ConnectionOptions.From(NetPulseSettings.Instance, Pulse.UserId, "Player");
        options.EncryptionMode = ClientEncryptionMode.Required;
        options.ServerPublicKeys = new[] { _serverPublicKey };
        await Pulse.Connect(options);
        Debug.Log($"Encrypted: {Pulse.Client.IsEncrypted}");
    }
}

ConnectionOptions.ValidateSecurity() returns a message for a missing or malformed key, or null when the options are fine. Pulse.Connect fails the operation with NetPulseReturnCode.InvalidConfiguration (-104) in that case and sends nothing. Pulse.Client.IsEncrypted is true once the handshake has finished.

If the handshake cannot finish, the connection ends with one of two disconnect reasons: SecureHandshakeTimeout (the server did not answer within Handshake Timeout, which also happens with a wrong server key or pre-shared key, because the server stays silent on purpose) and SecureHandshakeFailed (the answer could not be verified, or the session was closed because it reached its counter limit). A key that the server does not know looks like a timeout, not like a rejection.

The server public key is not secret, but it has to be the real one: it is what protects the client from a man in the middle. The pre-shared key and the connection key travel inside the build and can be extracted, see the threat model in Security.

Encryption adds 26 bytes to every datagram (more with Padding Block). The cryptography is C# code in the package and works with Mono and IL2CPP on every platform that supports System.Net.Sockets. WebGL, which has no UDP, is outside the scope of this transport.

docs.title: States and events
docs.text:
Pulse.State is a NetState. Pulse.IsConnected is true in every state except Disconnected, Connecting and Authenticating, so it also stays true while you are in a lobby or a room.

State When Disconnected Start state; after Disconnect(), a failed connect or a lost connection Connecting After Connect(), until the UDP link is up Authenticating The link is up and the server is checking the AppId, the protocol version and the token Connected Authenticated, outside any lobby or room InLobby After JoinLobby() JoiningRoom While a create or join request is pending InRoom After a successful create or join Leaving While LeaveRoom() is pending

NetState.Disconnecting is declared for later use and is not set by the current client. Connect() while the state is not Disconnected fails at once with InvalidState.

Every notification exists in three equivalent forms. Use whichever fits the script:

  1. C# events on Pulse.Events, for example Pulse.Events.OnJoinedRoom += Handler;.
  2. A MonoBehaviour that derives from NetPulseCallbacks. It registers itself in OnEnable, unregisters in OnDisable, and you override only the methods you need.
  3. Any object that implements one or more callback interfaces and is registered with Pulse.AddCallbackTarget(this) and Pulse.RemoveCallbackTarget(this).
using System.Collections.Generic;
using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class NetworkLog : NetPulseCallbacks
{
    public override void OnConnected() => Debug.Log("Connected");

    public override void OnDisconnected(string cause) => Debug.Log($"Disconnected: {cause}");

    public override void OnRoomListUpdate(IReadOnlyList<RoomInfo> rooms) => Debug.Log($"{rooms.Count} rooms");
}

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class RoomWatcher : MonoBehaviour, IRoomCallbacks
{
    private void OnEnable() => Pulse.AddCallbackTarget(this);

    private void OnDisable() => Pulse.RemoveCallbackTarget(this);

    public void OnPlayerEnteredRoom(Player player) => Debug.Log($"{player.NickName} entered");

    public void OnPlayerLeftRoom(Player player) => Debug.Log($"{player.NickName} left");

    public void OnRoomPropertiesChanged(NetPulse.Common.PropertyTable changed)
    {
    }

    public void OnPlayerPropertiesChanged(Player player, NetPulse.Common.PropertyTable changed)
    {
    }

    public void OnMasterClientSwitched(Player newMaster) => Debug.Log($"New master: {newMaster.NickName}");
}

Callbacks run on the main thread. An exception in one handler is logged and the others still run. The full list:

Event on Pulse.Events Interface Arguments OnStateChanged none (use Pulse.StateChanged) NetState OnConnected INetPulseConnectionCallbacks none OnDisconnected INetPulseConnectionCallbacks string cause OnJoinedLobby, OnLeftLobby ILobbyCallbacks none OnRoomListUpdate ILobbyCallbacks IReadOnlyList<RoomInfo> OnCreatedRoom, OnJoinedRoom, OnLeftRoom IMatchmakingCallbacks none OnCreateRoomFailed, OnJoinRoomFailed, OnJoinRandomFailed IMatchmakingCallbacks short returnCode, string message OnPlayerEnteredRoom, OnPlayerLeftRoom IRoomCallbacks Player OnRoomPropertiesChanged IRoomCallbacks PropertyTable changed OnPlayerPropertiesChanged IRoomCallbacks Player, PropertyTable changed OnMasterClientSwitched IRoomCallbacks Player newMaster OnOwnershipRequest IOwnershipCallbacks NetworkObject, Player requester OnOwnershipChanged IOwnershipCallbacks NetworkObject, Player previous, Player current OnOwnershipFailed IOwnershipCallbacks NetworkObject, short returnCode, string message OnNetworkSceneLoaded ISceneCallbacks string sceneName OnEvent IOnEventCallback byte code, int senderActorId, object data

NetPulseCallbacks implements all of the interfaces except that its methods are virtual and empty. OnEvent carries your own event codes 0 to 199 only (see the low-level API).

docs.title: Disconnecting and disconnect reasons
docs.text:
Pulse.Disconnect() closes the connection from your side. The OnDisconnected event (and the failed operations) carry a reason string:

Reason Cause Client disconnect You called Pulse.Disconnect() or the application quit Timeout No packets arrived for 10 seconds ConnectionFailed The handshake got no answer HostUnreachable, NetworkUnreachable, UnknownHost The address could not be reached or resolved RemoteConnectionClose The server closed the connection (a kick, a shutdown, a rejected token) ConnectionRejected The server refused the handshake, for example because of a wrong connection key InvalidProtocol The server speaks a different transport protocol version SecureHandshakeTimeout The secure handshake got no answer within Handshake Timeout: a wrong server key or pre-shared key, a server without encryption, or a lost network SecureHandshakeFailed The answer of the server could not be verified, or the encrypted session was closed RateLimited The server disconnected you for sending too many messages or bytes, or a message that was too large (the transport adds extra data after the reason, for example RemoteConnectionClose:RateLimited) AuthTimeout, TooManyAuthAttempts The server disconnected you because you did not authenticate in time, or failed too often Failed to open a UDP socket The local socket could not be opened A server message An authentication failure passes the server's text (for example for a wrong AppId)

Most strings are LiteNetLib's DisconnectReason names. When the connection drops, every pending operation fails with NetPulseReturnCode.Disconnected (-101), the room and the room list are cleared, network objects are destroyed locally, and the state returns to Disconnected. OnLeftRoom is raised first if you were in a room, then OnDisconnected.

To reconnect, call Pulse.Connect() again. A common pattern is to start it from OnDisconnected after a short delay.

docs.title: Operation errors
docs.text:
Every request has a timeout (Request Timeout, 10 seconds by default). Client-side failures use NetPulseReturnCode:

Code Name Meaning -100 Timeout The server did not answer in time -101 Disconnected The connection was lost or was never up -102 InvalidState The call is not allowed in the current state, for example joining a room while Disconnected

Server answers use the codes listed in codes and keys, for example AuthenticationFailed (-32), VersionMismatch (-30) and InvalidAppId (-31). Awaited operations throw NetPulseException with a ReturnCode; others expose Error.

docs.title: Connection quality and replacing the transport
docs.text:
Pulse.RoundTripTimeMs is the round-trip time of the UDP link. Pulse.ServerTime is the estimated server clock (see ticks and time).

Pulse.UseTransport(INetTransport) swaps the transport, for example for a WebSocket transport on WebGL. It must be called while disconnected and before Connect(). It resets the client, so register callbacks afterwards. The default transport is LiteNetLibTransport.

docs.title: IL2CPP
docs.text: NetPulse works with IL2CPP and managed code stripping at any stripping level. You do not need [Preserve] attributes or your own link.xml for [NetRpc] methods, [Synced] fields, NetworkBehaviour subclasses, INetSerializable types, [NetSerializable] types or INetMessage types. Two mechanisms keep them alive.

docs.title: Layer 1: the attributes
docs.text: [NetRpc], [Synced] and [NetSerializable] derive from UnityEngine.Scripting.PreserveAttribute. Unity documents that attribute as subclassable and honored by the linker, so a member marked with them survives stripping by itself.

docs.title: Layer 2: a generated link.xml
docs.text:
At build time the editor class NetPulseLinkerProcessor (an IUnityLinkerProcessor) finds your code through Unity's TypeCache and writes Library/NetPulse/link.xml. Unity's linker reads it together with its own files. The processor looks at the player assemblies without test assemblies, and for each of your assemblies it preserves:

  • every method marked [NetRpc], with its signature
  • every [Synced] field
  • every non-abstract NetworkBehaviour subclass, with its OnSerialize override and the generated RegisterSyncVars and InvokeGeneratedRpc methods
  • every type that implements INetSerializable
  • every [NetSerializable] type and every INetMessage type, with their generated NetWrite and NetRead methods

The three package assemblies, NetPulse.Runtime, NetPulse.Common and NetPulse.LiteNetLib, are preserved completely. They need an explicit entry because Unity does not read link.xml files that live inside packages.

The shape of the result:

<linker>
  <assembly fullname="NetPulse.Runtime" preserve="all" />
  <assembly fullname="NetPulse.Common" preserve="all" />
  <assembly fullname="NetPulse.LiteNetLib" preserve="all" />
  <assembly fullname="Assembly-CSharp">
    <type fullname="Hero">
      <method signature="System.Void Hit(System.Int32,UnityEngine.Vector3,NetPulse.NetRpcInfo)" />
      <method name="InvokeGeneratedRpc" />
    </type>
  </assembly>
</linker>

docs.title: Previewing it
docs.text:
Choose NetPulse > Tools > Preview IL2CPP link.xml. The editor writes the same content that a build would use to Library/NetPulse/link.preview.xml, prints it to the console and reveals the file. Use it to check that a type you care about is listed, for example after moving code into a new assembly definition.

A type is listed only if its assembly is part of the player build. Editor-only assemblies and test assemblies are left out on purpose.

docs.title: When something is still missing
docs.text:
If a reflection-based call cannot find an RPC method, the error names the type and the method and points back to this mechanism. In practice this means a custom build step bypassed the NetPulse linker processor (for example a build pipeline that replaces the additional link files). Check the preview and make sure the Library/NetPulse/link.xml is passed to the linker.

For generated RPCs, a missing dispatch usually has a different cause: the class is not partial, or the source generator is not active for the assembly. The error then says so. See analyzers and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The client is the Unity package com.netpulse.unity (version 0.4). It supports Unity 2021.3 LTS through Unity 6000.x, uses plain C# 9 and runs on the main thread, and it works with both Mono and IL2CPP. You also need a running NetPulse server; see getting started.

docs.title: Install with the Package Manager
docs.text:
1. Open Window > Package Manager.
  2. Click + and choose Install package from git URL....
  3. Paste this URL and confirm:
https://github.com/Klobiroff/NetPulse-Unity.git?path=Packages/com.netpulse.unity

The repository is private for now, so Unity needs git access. Install a git client, make sure git is on your PATH, and sign in to GitHub with an account that can read the repository (Git Credential Manager does this on Windows and macOS). If the Package Manager reports an authentication error, run git ls-remote https://github.com/Klobiroff/NetPulse-Unity.git in a terminal to check that your credentials work.

You can add the same line to Packages/manifest.json instead:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "com.netpulse.unity": "https://github.com/Klobiroff/NetPulse-Unity.git?path=Packages/com.netpulse.unity"
  }
}

To pin a version, append # and a tag, branch or commit hash to the URL.

docs.title: Copy the folder instead
docs.text: If git access is a problem, copy the com.netpulse.unity folder into your project's Packages folder. Unity treats it as an embedded package. Copy the whole folder including the .meta files, because the source generator DLL in Runtime/Analyzers relies on its import settings. As an alternative, use Add package from disk... in the Package Manager and select the folder's package.json.

docs.title: Assemblies
docs.text:
The package defines three assemblies: NetPulse.Runtime, NetPulse.Common (the protocol and serialization code, which is synced from the server repository, so do not edit it) and NetPulse.LiteNetLib (the vendored transport, LiteNetLib 1.3.5). Scripts in the default Assembly-CSharp reference them automatically.

If your code lives in its own assembly definition, add references to NetPulse.Runtime and NetPulse.Common. The source generator runs for every assembly that references NetPulse.Runtime, and the code it writes uses types from NetPulse.Common.

docs.title: Create the settings asset
docs.text:
Open Project Settings > NetPulse, or choose NetPulse > Create Settings Asset. Unity creates Assets/Resources/NetPulseSettings.asset. Set the host, the port (UDP 5055 by default), the AppId and the AppVersion. If the server is configured with an AppId, the client's AppId must equal it. The AppVersion is your own build version string; the server does not check it. Every field is described in settings and editor.

Without the asset, Pulse.Connect() still works with built-in defaults (host 127.0.0.1, port 5055), which is enough for a local test.

docs.title: Input System
docs.text: The package itself reads no input. The Basic sample does, and its scripts compile against whichever input backend your project uses. They use the Input System package when ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM is defined and the legacy Input Manager otherwise. If Project Settings > Player > Active Input Handling is set to Input System Package (New) or Both, install the com.unity.inputsystem package, or the sample scripts will not compile.

docs.title: The Basic sample
docs.text:
The sample is an IMGUI demo. It connects, lists rooms, creates and joins rooms, and spawns a player with generated RPCs, a SyncVar health value, a typed chat message, a typed room score, tick-based movement, master-only scene loading and a shared Takeover cube.

  1. Open Window > Package Manager, select NetPulse, open the Samples tab and import Basic.
  2. Choose NetPulse > Samples > Build Basic Sample Scene. This creates the settings asset if it is missing, a player prefab, the prefab registry and two scenes (BasicSample and BasicSampleArena) under Assets/NetPulse Basic Sample, and adds both scenes to Build Settings.
  3. Start a server, open BasicSample and press Play. Run a second instance (a standalone build, or a virtual player from Unity's Multiplayer Play Mode) to see two players.

Controls in the sample: WASD moves, Space sends an RPC, H damages your own SyncVar health, and E takes the shared cube, which you then move with the arrow keys.

docs.title: Running the package tests
docs.text:
The package includes tests in Tests/Runtime (serialization, the client on a fake transport, messages, typed keys, ticks, async helpers, network scenes, stats, SyncVar, generated RPCs, hooks and ownership) and in Tests/Editor. They are visible in the Test Runner when the package is listed under testables in Packages/manifest.json. A package that is embedded in Packages is already testable.

The ownership tests create GameObjects and use [UnityTest], so run them from the Test Runner in Play Mode.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with connecting, then matchmaking. If you know Photon, migrating from PUN maps the concepts you already have.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: NetworkBehaviour adds a set of virtual hooks to the usual Unity callbacks. This page lists each hook, when it runs and what is guaranteed about the order. Everything runs on the main thread.

docs.title: The hooks
Creation and spawn
docs.text:
1. Unity runs Awake and OnEnable. In NetworkObject.Awake the object collects its NetworkBehaviours (numbering them in hierarchy order) and registers their SyncVars. Unity does not define the order between Awake calls of different components, so do not read ViewId or IsMine in your own Awake. Use OnNetworkSpawned.
  2. OnNetworkSpawned runs exactly once per object, on every behaviour in hierarchy order. For an object you create with Pulse.Instantiate, it has already run when Instantiate returns. For an object owned by someone else, it normally runs right after the spawn arrives, in the same frame as Awake and OnEnable and before Start.
  3. If the object belongs to another player and has state to receive (SyncVar, [Synced] fields or OnSerialize), OnNetworkSpawned waits until the first state update has been applied, or one second at most. The first thing your code sees is then real data and not field defaults. In this case Start may run before it.
  4. OnNetworkSpawned always runs before the first OnNetworkTick of that object. An object that has not been announced yet gets no ticks.

Scene objects register in OnEnable, whether or not you are in a room. If the client is outside a room at that time, IsMine is true and OnNetworkSpawned runs at once. After you join as a non-master, IsMine becomes false without any ownership callback. Do setup that depends on who owns a scene object after OnJoinedRoom.

docs.title: Ownership change
docs.text:
The server announces the new owner. Then, for each behaviour of the object, in hierarchy order:

  1. OnOwnerChanged(previous, current)
  2. OnOwnershipGained() if you became the owner, or OnOwnershipLost() if you stopped being one

After all behaviours have been handled, the object raises NetworkObject.OwnershipChanged, and then Pulse.Events.OnOwnershipChanged (and IOwnershipCallbacks.OnOwnershipChanged) fire. The event is raised once for the object, not once per behaviour. Inside every hook, IsMine and Owner already show the new owner.

An object that a late joiner has only just created and is still waiting for its first state can receive OnOwnerChanged before its OnNetworkSpawned. Do not assume the spawn hook has run in OnOwnerChanged.

docs.title: Master change
docs.text:
When the server announces a new master:

  1. OnMasterChanged(previous, current) is called on every behaviour of every object whose OnNetworkSpawned has run. For a scene object without an explicit owner (which the master owns), OnOwnershipGained() or OnOwnershipLost() follows on the same behaviour if you became or stopped being the master.
  2. After all objects, Pulse.Events.OnMasterClientSwitched(newMaster) is raised.

docs.title: Despawn
docs.text: OnNetworkDespawned is called from the NetworkObject's OnDestroy, and only if OnNetworkSpawned had run. Unity does not fix the order of OnDestroy between components, so a behaviour's own OnDestroy can run before or after it. Release network-related resources in OnNetworkDespawned and plain resources in OnDestroy.

docs.title: Where NetPulse runs in the frame
docs.text:
A hidden runner object ([NetPulse], created on first use and kept across scenes) updates the client with execution order -1000, before your scripts' Update:

  1. It polls the transport. Everything that arrived is dispatched now: spawns, RPCs, state updates, property changes, ownership and master events, and your callbacks.
  2. It runs the network tick loop: OnNetworkTick for every spawned object, then the state sends of the tick (ticks and time).
  3. Your Update, LateUpdate and coroutines run afterwards, and see the data that arrived in step 1.

While a network scene is loading, room events are queued and dispatched afterwards in the original order (scenes).

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text: Everyday code does not need this page. The older, string-and-byte-code API is still supported and unchanged, and you meet it when you maintain 0.2 code, build tools, or need something the typed API does not offer. It covers reflection RPCs, raw events with byte codes, hand-registered serializers, interest groups and the transport.

docs.title: Reflection RPCs
docs.text:
CallRpc(methodName, target, arguments) calls a [NetRpc] method by its name. Use it when the name is only known at runtime, as in health.Send("Heal", 5) below:

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed partial class Health : NetworkBehaviour
{
    [Synced] private int _hp = 100;

    public int Hp => _hp;

    public void Send(string rpcName, int amount) => CallRpc(rpcName, RpcTarget.All, amount);

    [NetRpc]
    private void TakeDamage(int amount, NetRpcInfo info)
    {
        _hp -= amount;
        Debug.Log($"{info.Sender?.NickName} dealt {amount}");
    }

    [NetRpc]
    private void Heal(int amount) => _hp += amount;
}

How it differs from the generated Rpc.X():

  • The method is found with reflection, and the arguments travel as dynamically typed values. They can be anything PropertyTable values can be (rooms and properties) plus registered types. The receiver converts them to the parameter types.
  • The target is the argument you pass. The target in the attribute is not used. Delivery and OwnerOnly from the attribute are honored.
  • A wrong argument count logs an error and sends nothing. An unknown name logs an error that points to the likely cause (a typo, a missing attribute, or IL2CPP stripping, see IL2CPP).
  • When the name is a literal or a nameof expression and a valid [NetRpc] method with that name exists, the analyzer reports NP0011 and suggests the generated call, for example Rpc.TakeDamage(amount).

Reflection RPCs and generated RPCs both travel as event 242, with a different kind byte and argument layout (wire protocol).

docs.title: Raw events
docs.text:
Pulse.RaiseEvent(code, data, options) sends an event with a byte code from 0 to 199. A larger code throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Codes 230 to 250 belong to the system: 230 to 237 are server notifications, 240 to 245 carry spawns, destroys, RPCs, state, typed messages and master variables, and 250 reports errors.

using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class Flares : NetPulseCallbacks
{
    private const byte FlareEvent = 10;

    public void Launch(Vector3 position)
    {
        var options = new RaiseEventOptions
        {
            Receivers = ReceiverGroup.All,
            Delivery = DeliveryMode.ReliableUnordered
        };
        Pulse.RaiseEvent(FlareEvent, position, options);
    }

    public override void OnEvent(byte eventCode, int senderActorId, object data)
    {
        if (eventCode == FlareEvent && data is Vector3 position)
        {
            Debug.Log($"Flare from actor {senderActorId} at {position}");
        }
    }
}

RaiseEventOptions:

Property Default Meaning Receivers Others Others, All (the sender too), MasterClient, or Targets (the actors in TargetActors) TargetActors none Actor ids for Targets InterestGroup 0 Limit to a group, see below Caching DoNotCache Cache behavior, see below Delivery ReliableOrdered Transport mode

The event arrives as Pulse.Events.OnEvent(code, senderActorId, data) or through IOnEventCallback. Only your own codes 0 to 199 are reported there. Outside a room, RaiseEvent does nothing.

Caching options:

CachingOption Effect DoNotCache Deliver only AddToRoomCache Deliver and store. The server replays stored events to players who join later. They are removed when their sender leaves. AddToRoomCacheGlobal Like AddToRoomCache, but the event stays after the sender leaves RemoveFromRoomCache Remove every stored event with this code. Nothing is delivered. RemoveFromCacheForActorsLeft Remove stored events whose sender is no longer in the room. Nothing is delivered.

docs.title: Custom types and NetTypeRegistry
docs.text:
data and RPC arguments can be null, bool, byte, short, int, long, float, double, string, Guid, byte[], int[], float[], string[], object[], a PropertyTable or an IDictionary<string, object> with string keys. The Unity types Vector2, Vector3, Quaternion, Color, Vector2Int and Vector3Int are registered at start-up under type codes 100 to 105. Other types must be registered, or the send throws a serialization exception.

For new code, mark the type [NetSerializable] and the generator registers it for you (messages). To register a type by hand, pick an unused code from 100 to 199 and use the same code on every client:

using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public struct Checkpoint
{
    public int Index;
    public float Time;
}

public static class CheckpointSerializer
{
    public const byte Code = 120;

    [RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.BeforeSceneLoad)]
    private static void Register() => NetTypeRegistry.Register<Checkpoint>(
        Code,
        static (writer, value) =>
        {
            writer.WriteInt(value.Index);
            writer.WriteFloat(value.Time);
        },
        static reader => new Checkpoint { Index = reader.ReadInt(), Time = reader.ReadFloat() });
}

NetTypeRegistry also has RegisterExtended<T>(ushort id, ...) for the 16-bit ids that generated code uses, IsRegistered(code) and Unregister(code). Registering a code twice for different types throws. NetWriter and NetReader offer WriteInt, WriteFloat, WriteString and the matching Read methods for all primitives, and the extension methods of NetPulse add the Unity types.

docs.title: State by hand
docs.text: [Synced] fields, OnSerialize(NetStream) and SerializeDelivery are part of this older layer and are fully described in state sync. String property keys (room.SetProperty("map", "forest"), SetProperties(delta, expected)) are covered in rooms and properties.

docs.title: Interest groups
docs.text:
An interest group limits who receives an event. Group 0 means everyone. Any other group number reaches only the players who subscribed to it:

using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class Zone : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private byte _group = 5;

    public void Enter()
    {
        var add = new byte[] { _group };
        Pulse.ChangeInterestGroups(add, null);
    }

    public void Exit()
    {
        var remove = new byte[] { _group };
        Pulse.ChangeInterestGroups(null, remove);
    }
}
  • Set the group on an event with RaiseEventOptions.InterestGroup, on a network object with its Interest Group field, and on a spawn with the interestGroup argument of Pulse.Instantiate.
  • Group filtering applies to Others and All. Events for the master client or for specific actors ignore it.
  • Subscribing needs a room, and does nothing in offline mode. Subscriptions are dropped when a player becomes inactive.
  • Cached events are replayed once, when a player joins, and only those whose group the player has at that moment. Subscribing later does not retrieve what was cached before.

docs.title: Transport and protocol
docs.text: Pulse.UseTransport(INetTransport) replaces the default LiteNetLibTransport. The interface has Connect, Send, Poll and Disconnect plus the Connected, Disconnected and DataReceived events and the properties IsConnected and RoundTripTimeMs. It must be set while disconnected. The wire format is described in wire protocol.

docs.title: Matchmaking
docs.text: Matchmaking is how players end up in the same room: browse a room list in the lobby, join a room by name, create one, or let the server pick a random room that matches your filter. Every call returns a NetOperation<Room>, so you can await it. Call these after Pulse.Connect() has completed (connecting).

docs.title: The lobby and the room list
docs.text:
Joining the lobby is optional. Do it when you want a live room browser:

using System.Collections.Generic;
using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class RoomBrowser : NetPulseCallbacks
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        await Pulse.Connect();
        await Pulse.JoinLobby();
    }

    public override void OnRoomListUpdate(IReadOnlyList<RoomInfo> rooms)
    {
        foreach (var room in rooms)
        {
            var map = room.LobbyProperties?.Get<string>("map");
            Debug.Log($"{room.Name} {room.PlayerCount}/{room.MaxPlayers} open={room.IsOpen} map={map}");
        }
    }
}

JoinLobby() works from the Connected state and moves the client to InLobby. The server sends the full list at once and then deltas about once a second. The client merges them, and Pulse.LobbyRooms always holds the current list sorted by name. OnRoomListUpdate fires after each update with that merged list.

If you only need a snapshot, call GetRoomList() from Connected or InLobby. It returns NetOperation<IReadOnlyList<RoomInfo>>. LeaveLobby() stops the updates and clears LobbyRooms.

A RoomInfo has Name, PlayerCount, MaxPlayers, IsOpen and LobbyProperties. The list contains visible rooms only. LobbyProperties holds just the custom properties whose keys the room creator listed in RoomOptions.LobbyProperties. This keeps the list small and is also the set that random matchmaking filters on (below).

Joining a room from the lobby leaves the client InRoom. After you leave the room the state is Connected, so call JoinLobby() again to resume the list.

docs.title: RoomOptions
docs.text:
RoomOptions (in NetPulse.Common) describes a room at creation time:

Property Default Meaning MaxPlayers 0 Player limit, 0 for unlimited. A byte, so at most 255. IsVisible true Whether the room appears in the room list. IsOpen true Whether new players may join. CustomProperties none Initial room properties (rooms and properties). LobbyProperties none Keys of CustomProperties that are copied into RoomInfo.LobbyProperties. Plugin none Name of the server plugin that runs this room (plugins). PlayerTtlMs 0 How long the server keeps the slot of a disconnected player. See below. EmptyRoomTtlMs 0 How long an empty room stays alive. 0 closes it at once.

The room can change IsOpen, IsVisible and MaxPlayers later through the reserved room properties _isOpen, _isVisible and _maxPlayers, which only the master client may set. For example, room.SetProperty("_isOpen", false) stops new joins once a match starts.

docs.title: Create, join, join or create
docs.text:
using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class JoinExample : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        await Pulse.Connect();

        var options = new RoomOptions
        {
            MaxPlayers = 4,
            CustomProperties = new PropertyTable { ["map"] = "forest", ["mode"] = "ctf" },
            LobbyProperties = new[] { "map", "mode" }
        };

        var room = await Pulse.JoinOrCreateRoom("arena", options);
        Debug.Log($"{room.Name}: {room.PlayerCount} players, master is {room.MasterClient.NickName}");
    }
}
Call Behavior Typical failure codes CreateRoom(name, options, playerProperties) Creates the room. An empty name makes the server pick one. RoomAlreadyExists JoinRoom(name, playerProperties) Joins an existing room. RoomNotFound, RoomFull, RoomClosed JoinOrCreateRoom(name, options, playerProperties) Joins the room if it exists, creates it with options otherwise. RoomFull, RoomClosed JoinRandomRoom(expectedProperties, expectedMaxPlayers, createOptions, playerProperties) Joins a random matching room. NoMatchFound

All arguments after the name are optional. playerProperties is a PropertyTable that becomes the local player's properties at the moment of joining, so other clients see them in OnPlayerEnteredRoom. The codes are ReturnCode values from NetPulse.Common; the full list is in codes and keys.

A successful call completes with the Room. By then Pulse.CurrentRoom, Pulse.LocalPlayer and the player list are filled, the server clock is synchronized, and the state is InRoom. Events fire in this order: OnCreatedRoom (only if this call created the room), then OnJoinedRoom, then the operation completes. A failed call raises one of OnCreateRoomFailed, OnJoinRoomFailed or OnJoinRandomFailed with the code and message, and the awaited operation throws a NetPulseException. A user can be in only one room at a time, and joining while already in a room fails.

using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class JoinWithErrors : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        await Pulse.Connect();

        try
        {
            await Pulse.JoinRoom("arena");
        }
        catch (NetPulseException e) when (e.ReturnCode == ReturnCode.RoomNotFound)
        {
            await Pulse.CreateRoom("arena", new RoomOptions { MaxPlayers = 4 });
        }
        catch (NetPulseException e)
        {
            Debug.LogError($"Join failed ({e.ReturnCode}): {e.Message}");
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Joining a random room
docs.text:
JoinRandomRoom looks at rooms that are visible, open and not full. It keeps those whose LobbyProperties match expectedProperties (every listed key must be equal) and whose MaxPlayers equals expectedMaxPlayers (0 means any), picks one at random and tries to join it. If nothing fits, it creates a new room with createOptions and a generated name, or fails with NoMatchFound when createOptions is null.

using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class QuickMatch : MonoBehaviour
{
    private async void Start()
    {
        await Pulse.Connect();

        var filter = new PropertyTable { ["mode"] = "ctf" };
        var fallback = new RoomOptions
        {
            MaxPlayers = 8,
            CustomProperties = new PropertyTable { ["mode"] = "ctf" },
            LobbyProperties = new[] { "mode" }
        };

        var room = await Pulse.JoinRandomRoom(filter, 0, fallback);
        Debug.Log($"Playing in {room.Name}");
    }
}

The filter can only see lobby properties. A key you filter on must be listed in RoomOptions.LobbyProperties of the rooms you want to find, as mode is above.

docs.title: Leaving and rejoining
docs.text:
await Pulse.LeaveRoom();

LeaveRoom() returns to Connected. All network objects of the room are destroyed locally and OnLeftRoom fires. Calling it outside a room fails with InvalidState.

LeaveRoom(becomeInactive: true) and a lost connection leave your slot reserved instead of removing you, if the room was created with PlayerTtlMs other than 0. A positive value keeps the slot for that many milliseconds. Other clients get OnPlayerLeftRoom with player.IsInactive set to true, and your objects stay in the room. When the same UserId calls JoinRoom for that room before the time runs out, the server gives the old ActorId back, and the other clients get OnPlayerEnteredRoom again. With PlayerTtlMs at 0, leaving always removes the player, and the objects they own are destroyed for everyone.

For rejoin to work, the UserId must stay the same, so keep Persist User Id on (connecting).

docs.title: The room you are in
docs.text:
Once joined, these are available from Pulse:

Member Meaning Pulse.IsInRoom True in the InRoom state Pulse.CurrentRoom The Room, or null Pulse.LocalPlayer, Pulse.LocalActorId You Pulse.IsMasterClient Whether you are the master

Room and Player are covered in rooms and properties. To wait until enough players have arrived, use Pulse.WaitForPlayersAsync (async).

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: A typed message is the simplest way to tell everyone in a room something that does not belong to a particular object: a chat line, a "round started" notice, a vote. You define a struct or class, send it with Pulse.Send, and receive it with Pulse.On<T>. There are no event codes and no registration calls, because the source generator writes the serialization code at compile time.

docs.title: Define, send, receive
docs.text:
Declare the message as a partial type that implements INetMessage:

using System;
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

public partial struct ChatMessage : INetMessage
{
    public string Text;
    public int Channel;
}

public sealed class Chat : MonoBehaviour
{
    private IDisposable _subscription;

    private void OnEnable() => _subscription = Pulse.On<ChatMessage>((message, sender) => Debug.Log($"{sender?.NickName}: {message.Text}"));

    private void OnDisable() => _subscription?.Dispose();

    public void Say(string text) => Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = text, Channel = 1 }, RpcTarget.All);
}

Pulse.On<T> returns an IDisposable. Dispose it to unsubscribe. The handler gets the message and the Player who sent it. The sender can be null if that player has already left. You can subscribe at any time, including before you are in a room.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
Pulse.Send has three shapes. All of them need to be called while you are in a room; otherwise they log a warning and send nothing.

using NetPulse;
using NetPulse.Common;
using UnityEngine;

public partial struct ChatMessage : INetMessage
{
    public string Text;
}

public sealed class SendExamples : MonoBehaviour
{
    private void Send(Player somePlayer)
    {
        Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = "hi" });
        Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = "all" }, RpcTarget.All);
        Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = "psst" }, somePlayer);
        Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = "welcome" }, RpcTarget.OthersBuffered);
        Pulse.Send(new ChatMessage { Text = "fast" }, RpcTarget.Others, new MessageOptions { Delivery = DeliveryMode.Unreliable });
    }
}
Overload Meaning Send(message) To everyone else (RpcTarget.Others) Send(message, target) To a target group Send(message, target, options) Same, with MessageOptions Send(message, player, options) To one player

The targets:

RpcTarget Delivered to Others Everyone except you All Everyone, you included. Your own handlers run immediately, inside the Send call. MasterClient The master. If you are the master, only your own handlers run and nothing is sent. OthersBuffered Everyone else now, and every player who joins later (the server caches the message) AllBuffered Like OthersBuffered, and your own handlers run too Owner Not valid for messages (there is no object). It logs a warning.

Sending to a Player who is the local player runs only your own handlers.

docs.title: MessageOptions
docs.text:
MessageOptions has two settings:

  • Delivery: ReliableOrdered (the default), ReliableUnordered, UnreliableSequenced or Unreliable. Use an unreliable mode for data where a lost packet does not matter because a newer one follows.
  • Caching: DoNotCache (the default) or one of the CachingOption values. The buffered targets above set the cache for you. Caching = RemoveFromRoomCache removes all cached messages from the room, of every message type, and that message itself is not delivered.

Messages are not filtered by interest groups.

docs.title: Serializable types
docs.text:
A message type, and any type nested inside it, is described by its public instance fields and its public properties that have both a getter and a setter and are written as auto-properties. They are written in declaration order. Read-only fields, constants, statics and computed properties are skipped.

Supported field types:

  • bool, byte, sbyte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double, char, string, Guid, and enums
  • Vector2, Vector3, Vector4, Quaternion, Color, Color32, Vector2Int, Vector3Int, Rect
  • Player and NetworkObject (sent as the actor id or view id; the receiver gets null if the player or object is not known there)
  • one-dimensional arrays and List<T> of any of these
  • other types marked [NetSerializable] or implementing INetMessage
using System.Collections.Generic;
using NetPulse;
using UnityEngine;

[NetSerializable]
public partial struct Stats
{
    public int Hp;
    public bool Alive;
}

public partial class RoundSummary : INetMessage
{
    public Stats Winner;
    public Vector3[] Spawns;
    public List<string> Names;
    public Player Mvp { get; set; }
}

[NetSerializable] is the same mechanism for types that are not messages. Use it for values you pass as RPC arguments, store in properties or put inside other messages. The rules:

  • The type must be partial, and so must any type that contains it.
  • It cannot be generic.
  • A class needs a parameterless constructor. It is written with a leading null flag, so a null class instance arrives as null. A struct has no such flag.
  • null and empty arrays or lists look the same on the wire, and a null collection arrives as an empty one.

The analyzer reports a violation as a compile error (analyzers). The message id is a hash of the type's full name, so renaming or moving a type changes it, and both sides must run the same version. A receiver that gets an id it does not know logs one warning and ignores the message.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
• Several handlers for one type are allowed. They run in the order they were added.
  • An exception in a handler is logged, and the remaining handlers still run.
  • Messages that arrive while a network scene is loading are held and replayed afterwards (scenes).

docs.title: Network objects
docs.text: A network object is a GameObject that exists in every client of a room and has the same identity everywhere. You build one from a NetworkObject component plus your own NetworkBehaviour scripts. This page covers creating, destroying and finding them. State, RPCs and ownership have their own pages.

docs.title: Setting up a prefab
docs.text:
1. Add a NetworkObject to the root of the prefab.
  2. Add your NetworkBehaviour scripts, and components such as NetworkTransform, to the root or its children.
  3. Save the prefab under Assets. NetPulse adds it to the NetworkPrefabRegistry automatically.

The NetworkObject inspector has these settings:

Setting Meaning Ownership Mode Fixed, Takeover or Request (ownership) Interest Group Events of this object reach only players subscribed to this group; 0 is everyone (low-level API) Persist Across Scenes Keep the object when the master loads a new network scene (scenes). The object must be a root object. Scene Object / Scene Id For objects placed in the scene (below)

NetworkObject finds every NetworkBehaviour on the object and its children, including inactive ones, once in Awake, and numbers them in hierarchy order. The number identifies the behaviour in the network traffic, so the hierarchy has to be the same on every client, and you cannot add a NetworkBehaviour to a networked object at runtime. An object can hold up to 256 behaviours.

docs.title: The prefab registry
docs.text:
Spawning sends a small id, not a name, so every client needs the same table of prefabs. That table is the NetworkPrefabRegistry asset, normally Assets/Resources/NetworkPrefabRegistry.asset, referenced by the Prefab Registry field of the settings.
